templates.title: Fine-tuning job outcomes per base model and method — retries counted once, cancellations shown apart
templates.subtopic: latest attempt per retry chain (DISTINCT ON), terminal state per job, LEAD over state events, percentile_cont with FILTER

sections.scenario: Customers of a cloud for open models start fine-tuning jobs on a dataset they uploaded, choosing a base model and a method: LoRA (a small adapter trained on top of the frozen base model) or a full fine-tune. A job first validates the dataset's format, then waits in a queue, then trains. When a job fails, the customer often fixes the problem and retries it. The fine-tuning team reviews outcomes per base model and method to see where jobs fail: at dataset validation (usually a format problem the customer can fix) or during training (more often the platform's problem), and how long jobs wait for capacity.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns base_model, method, jobs, completed, failed_validation, failed_training, cancelled, completion_rate, median_queue_minutes, one row per (base model, method) that has at least one job, ordered by base_model, method. A retry is a row of ft_jobs whose retry_of names the original job (always the first attempt, never another retry). The original and all its retries are one job, and it is counted once, by its latest attempt (largest created_at): that attempt's base model, method and outcome. An attempt's outcome is its terminal event: completed, validation_failed, failed (during training) or cancelled; failed_validation and failed_training count the second and third. completion_rate is completed ÷ (completed + failed_validation + failed_training), rounded to 3 decimals, NULL when that is 0. An attempt's minutes queued is the sum, over its queued events, of the minutes from that event to the attempt's next event. median_queue_minutes is percentile_cont(0.5) of the minutes queued of latest attempts that completed or failed, NULL if there are none. {{cancel_rule}} {{queue_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Timestamps are whole minutes in UTC. The sample has {{attempts}} attempts and {{events}} events; a real platform has many thousands of jobs a week.
sections.assumptions: Base models, tenants, methods, counts and timings are hypothetical. Job states are simplified to validating, validation_failed, queued, running, completed, failed and cancelled; a real pipeline has more (checkpointing, uploading the result). The data was extracted after every attempt in it had reached a terminal state. Datasets appear only through the outcome of the validation the customer asked for; nothing about their content is used.
sections.criteria: One job per retry chain, judged by its latest attempt (base model, method and outcome); one outcome per attempt even with duplicate terminal events; validation failures separated from training failures; cancelled jobs shown apart and outside the rate's denominator; minutes queued summed over every queued period and excluding validation; median over the right jobs, NULL when none; exact rounding; deterministic order; sensible answers on retries, resumes from checkpoints and incremental maintenance.

clarifications.q: A job failed at validation, was retried and completed. What do I count?
clarifications.a: One job, completed. The failed first attempt is not counted anywhere.

clarifications.q: Does retry_of ever point to another retry?
clarifications.a: No. Every retry names the original job, so one level of grouping is enough.

clarifications.q: Do cancelled jobs count in completion_rate?
clarifications.a: No. They are shown in cancelled and left out of the rate's denominator.

clarifications.q: Does time spent validating the dataset count as queued?
clarifications.a: No. Minutes queued start at a queued event and end at the attempt's next event, whatever it is.

clarifications.q: Which jobs feed the median?
clarifications.a: Jobs whose latest attempt completed or failed; jobs that failed validation never queued, and cancelled jobs are shown apart.

hints: COALESCE(retry_of, job_id) names each attempt's job; DISTINCT ON (that) … ORDER BY that, created_at DESC keeps the latest attempt.
The terminal event of an attempt is its latest event among the four terminal states; DISTINCT ON (job_id) again, so a terminal event delivered twice still gives one outcome.

LEAD(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY job_id ORDER BY event_ts) gives each event's next event; sum the gaps after queued events. percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …) FILTER (WHERE …) keeps the median to the right jobs.
followups: The team also wants the share of jobs that needed at least one retry before completing, per base model and method. Add it without counting a job twice.
A customer retries a failed LoRA job as a full fine-tune on a different base model. Which group should it count in, and what would the per-model view hide?

Jobs now write a checkpoint every N steps, and a failed job can resume from its last checkpoint instead of retrying from the start. How do you model resumes so minutes queued and outcomes stay honest?
At millions of events a month, how would you keep this report up to date incrementally as events arrive, including a late terminal event for a job already counted?

rules.ask: A terminal event was delivered twice. How many outcomes does your query count for that job, and how would you make the count immune to duplicates?
A job failed validation, was fixed and retried, and completed. Which attempt decides its outcome in your query, and which should?
How long did a job that spent 6 minutes validating and 40 minutes in the queue wait in your query, and what does the team want to measure?
Queue waits are long-tailed when capacity is short. Why might the median be the better headline here, and what would you show next to it?
A job is preempted and queued a second time. Does your query add both queued periods, and what happens when two events of one job share a timestamp?

templates.title: Dedicated endpoint replica-minutes per endpoint and UTC day — every started minute billed per running replica
templates.subtopic: step functions from change events (LEAD), expanding intervals to the minutes they touch, MAX per minute, idle filtering, day splitting

sections.scenario: A customer of a cloud for open models runs a dedicated endpoint: a model deployment reserved for them, with a number of replicas that the customer or an autoscaler changes over time. In this exercise the endpoint is billed per minute for each running replica (this exercise's rule; check current docs for real billing). The billing team produces each endpoint's daily replica-minutes and cost, and shows how many of those replica-minutes served no request at all, so customers can see what idle capacity costs them.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns day, endpoint_id, billed_replica_minutes, idle_replica_minutes, cost_usd for the report ({{report_days}}), one row per endpoint and UTC day with at least one billed replica-minute, ordered by day, endpoint_id. Each row of replica_events sets the endpoint's replica count to replicas from event_ts until the endpoint's next event; before an endpoint's first event its count is 0, and 0 means stopped. This exercise's billing rule: every clock minute (UTC, from :00 to the next :00) is billed for the largest number of replicas running at any moment in that minute, so a minute in which a replica started or stopped is billed in full. billed_replica_minutes sums that over the day's minutes. idle_replica_minutes sums it over the minutes in which the endpoint received no request (a request at request_ts belongs to the minute it falls in). cost_usd is billed_replica_minutes × price_per_replica_minute, rounded to 2 decimals. {{before_rule}} {{minute_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Timestamps are whole seconds in UTC. The report covers {{first_day}} to {{last_day}} inclusive. The sample has {{scale_events}} scale events and {{requests}} requests; a busy endpoint has many thousands of requests a minute, and a platform has many endpoints.
sections.assumptions: Endpoints, prices, replica counts and traffic are hypothetical, and the per-started-minute rule is this exercise's billing rule, not any provider's; check current docs. A replica counts as running from the event that starts it, whether or not it is ready to serve. Requests are only used to tell busy minutes from idle ones.
sections.criteria: The count from the last event at or before each moment, including events before the report; segments clipped to the report and split at UTC midnight; every minute billed at the largest count running in it, so started minutes are whole and a stop exactly on the minute bills nothing for that minute; idle replica-minutes as replicas × minutes with no request; stopped periods excluded; exact rounding of cost; deterministic order; a credible plan for month-scale computation and late events.

clarifications.q: The endpoint scaled from 2 to 4 replicas at 10:05:30. How is 10:05 billed?
clarifications.a: 4 replica-minutes. Four replicas ran during that minute, so it is billed for four.

clarifications.q: It stopped at exactly 10:07:00. Is 10:07 billed?
clarifications.a: No. At no moment from 10:07:00 to 10:08:00 was a replica running. 10:06 is billed in full.

clarifications.q: What makes a minute idle?
clarifications.a: No request at all for that endpoint between its :00 and the next :00. An idle minute on three replicas is three idle replica-minutes.

clarifications.q: A request arrived while the endpoint was stopped.
clarifications.a: It bills nothing; a stopped minute is not in either total.

clarifications.q: Should an endpoint-day with no billed minutes appear?
clarifications.a: No. Only endpoint-days with at least one billed replica-minute.

hints: Turn events into segments: LEAD(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY endpoint_id ORDER BY event_ts) is where a count stops applying; the last segment runs to the end of the report. Clip each segment to the report.
A segment from a to b touches the minutes from date_trunc('minute', a) up to the last minute that starts before b; generate_series over those minutes and take MAX(replicas) per endpoint and minute.
Build the set of minutes that had a request with date_trunc('minute', request_ts) and LEFT JOIN it; FILTER (WHERE … IS NULL) gives the idle sum.
followups: A month has 43 200 minutes per endpoint. How would you compute billed minutes from segments without expanding every minute, and where does the per-minute rule make that harder?
Customers ask why an endpoint that "scaled to zero at 10:07" was billed for 10:06. Write the explanation the invoice should carry.
Scale events arrive late from the control plane, sometimes after the day was invoiced. What do you do with the difference?
The team wants to show customers the replica-minutes they could have saved with a smaller minimum replica count. What would you compute, and what would you refuse to promise?

rules.ask: Your query measures running time in seconds. What does this exercise's rule bill for a replica that ran from 10:05:30 to 10:06:10, and what does yours?
How many rows does your grid make for 2 000 endpoints over a month, and which minutes can you skip?
The endpoint spiked from 2 to 6 replicas for 20 seconds inside one minute. What does your query bill for that minute?
An idle minute on three replicas: is that one idle unit or three in your query?
An endpoint was scaled to 2 replicas yesterday and has no event today. What does your query bill it for today?

templates.title: Adapter traffic on shared endpoints — requests per LoRA adapter, the base model's share, and adapters idle for 7 days
templates.subtopic: day × entity grid, ROW_NUMBER over an aggregate for the top item with ties, interval coverage of a trailing window, NOT EXISTS, string_agg

sections.scenario: On a cloud for open models, a customer can attach several LoRA adapters to one dedicated endpoint: every request names an adapter, or none to use the base model alone, and all of them share the endpoint's replicas. Each attached adapter takes memory on those replicas. The endpoint dashboard shows each day how traffic splits between the base model and the adapters, which adapter was busiest, and which adapters have sat attached for a week without serving anything, so the customer can detach them.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns day, endpoint_id, requests, base_share, adapters_used, busiest_adapter, idle_adapters: one row for every endpoint in adapter_attachments and every UTC day from {{first_day}} to {{last_day}}, ordered by day, endpoint_id. Only requests with status ok were served. requests counts the endpoint's served requests that day; base_share is the share of them with no adapter_id, rounded to 3 decimals (NULL with no requests). adapters_used counts distinct adapters with a served request that day, and busiest_adapter is the adapter with the most served requests that day, ties to the smaller adapter_id (NULL if none). idle_adapters lists, as adapter_ids in ascending order joined by ', ', the adapters for which one attachment row covers the whole 7 days ending that day (attached at or before 00:00 six days earlier, and not detached before the end of the day) and that served no request on this endpoint in those 7 days; NULL when there are none. {{status_rule}} {{attach_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Timestamps are whole seconds in UTC. A detachment time of NULL means still attached. Endpoints in this sample: {{endpoints}}; {{attachments}} attachment rows and {{requests}} requests.
sections.assumptions: Endpoints, adapters, attachment history and traffic are hypothetical. An adapter's memory cost is not modelled; the dashboard only lists candidates to detach. Request contents are never used, only which adapter a request named.
sections.criteria: A full endpoint × day grid; only served requests counted anywhere; correct base share and its NULL; busiest adapter with the stated tie rule; a 7-day window that starts at 00:00 six days earlier and includes that instant; idle only when a single attachment covers the whole window, per endpoint; a sorted list and NULL when empty; deterministic order; sensible answers on last-used, on-demand loading and pre-aggregation.

clarifications.q: Which 7 days are "the 7 days ending" on 2026-09-30?
clarifications.a: 2026-09-24 00:00 up to 2026-10-01 00:00. A request at exactly 2026-09-24 00:00:00 is inside the window.

clarifications.q: An adapter was attached three days ago and has never been called. Is it idle?
clarifications.a: Not by this rule. It has not been attached for the whole window, so it is not listed yet.

clarifications.q: An adapter was detached in the afternoon. Can it appear in that day's list?
clarifications.a: No. It was not attached until the end of the day.

clarifications.q: Two adapters tie for the most requests.
clarifications.a: The smaller adapter_id is the busiest.

clarifications.q: What if an endpoint had no requests on a day?
clarifications.a: It still gets a row: requests 0, base_share NULL, adapters_used 0, busiest_adapter NULL, and its idle list.

hints: Build the grid first: report days from generate_series CROSS JOIN the endpoints, then LEFT JOIN the served requests of that day, so empty days keep their row.
For the busiest adapter, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY day, endpoint_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, adapter_id) over the grouped counts, and keep rank 1.
For idle adapters, join attachments that cover the window and keep them with NOT EXISTS a served request in the window; string_agg(adapter_id, ', ' ORDER BY adapter_id) builds the list.
followups: The customer wants each idle adapter's last served request next to it, or "never". How would you add it?
Adapters are loaded into replica memory on demand and evicted when unused. How does that change what "idle" should mean on the dashboard?
An endpoint serves thousands of requests a second. Which daily aggregate would you maintain so this query never scans raw requests?
The same adapter is attached to two endpoints in different regions. Should the dashboard call it idle if one of them serves it? Argue both ways.

rules.ask: Which instant does your window start at for a report day, and is a request at exactly 00:00 six days earlier inside it?
An adapter was detached and attached again yesterday, and has not been called since. Has it been attached for the whole window in your query?
A call to an adapter was rejected because it was not attached. Should that count as the adapter being used, in this report and in a capacity report?
Two adapters tie for the most requests. Which does your query return, and is that deterministic across runs?
An endpoint had no served requests on one day. Does it still get a row in your query?

templates.title: Ordering a customer's own fine-tuning queue — the least total weighted completion time
templates.subtopic: exchange argument (Smith's ratio rule), exact ratio comparison by cross-multiplication, tie rules

sections.scenario: A customer of a cloud for open models has a fixed fine-tuning allocation that runs one job at a time, and a queue of jobs, each with an estimated number of minutes. The customer sets a weight per job for how much it matters to have that job finished early. The console offers to reorder the customer's own queue so that the sum, over jobs, of weight × the minute at which the job finishes is as small as possible.
sections.problem: Implement queue_order(jobs, running=None). jobs is a list of (job_id, minutes, weight) with integer minutes and weights. Jobs run one after another with no gaps, starting at minute 0; a job's completion time is the sum of the minutes of every job up to and including it. Return (order, total): order is the list of job ids in an order that minimises the total of weight × completion time, and total is that minimum. When two jobs have exactly the same ratio of minutes to weight, the one with the smaller job_id (string order) goes first. {{weight_rule}} {{running_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 60 000 jobs in the timing check. Trying every order is O(n!), and picking the best remaining job again and again is O(n²); one sort, O(n log n), is expected. Compare ratios exactly; do not trust floating-point division.
sections.assumptions: Minutes, weights and job ids are hypothetical. Estimates are taken as exact; how real job lengths are estimated is not part of this exercise. Only the customer's own queue is reordered; other customers' jobs are not involved.
sections.criteria: Sort by the ratio of minutes to weight, compared exactly by cross-multiplication; ties by job id; the total computed in exact integers; at Hard, zero-weight jobs last, an empty queue, and None for invalid input; at Very Hard, the running job kept first, None for an unknown running id, and values up to 10^9 handled without floats; O(n log n) with a clear exchange-argument proof; good answers on precedence, parallel machines and re-planning.

clarifications.q: Should I just run the shortest job first?
clarifications.a: Not when weights differ. A long job that matters a lot can belong before a short job that matters little.

clarifications.q: How do I compare two jobs?
clarifications.a: By minutes ÷ weight, smaller first. Compare m1 × w2 with m2 × w1 in integers, so equal ratios are recognised exactly.

clarifications.q: Do I return a tuple?
clarifications.a: Yes, (order, total) with order a list of job ids, or None where the statement says so.

clarifications.q: Which order do you want when several orders give the same minimum?
clarifications.a: Jobs with equal ratios go by job_id; with that rule the order is unique.

hints: Look at two adjacent jobs and swap them. Only their own two terms change. Which order is better, in terms of minutes and weights?
The swap argument says: job a goes before job b when minutes_a × weight_b < minutes_b × weight_a. Sort by that comparison (functools.cmp_to_key, or an exact key such as fractions.Fraction).
Ties by job_id make the answer unique, and integers keep the total exact however large it gets.
followups: Prove the exchange argument: why does any order with an adjacent pair out of ratio order have a strictly larger total, unless their ratios are equal?
Some jobs must run after another job of the same customer (for example, evaluation after training). What happens to the greedy, and what would you do for chains of jobs?
The allocation now runs two jobs at a time. Is the ratio rule still optimal? What would you try instead?
Estimates are often wrong. How would the console re-plan when a running job overruns, and how would you explain the new order to the customer?

rules.ask: Jobs (a, 10 minutes, weight 1) and (b, 30 minutes, weight 6). Which order does shortest-first give, and what are the two totals?
Weights and minutes can be near 10^9. Can two different ratios divide to the same float, and what does your tie rule do then?
How many orders are there for 20 jobs, and what property of an optimal order lets you avoid trying them?
Jobs (a, 700 minutes, weight 5) and (b, 70 minutes, weight 2). Which goes first by weight, and which by the total?
How does your comparison place a job with weight 0, and does it ever divide by zero?

templates.title: Structured output streams — the chunk where the JSON became complete, the first invalid character, or still incomplete
templates.subtopic: incremental state machine across chunk boundaries (bracket stack, string and escape states)

sections.scenario: An inference API for open models can stream a response in JSON mode: the text arrives in small chunks, and a client wants to act as soon as the JSON object is complete, or stop as soon as the text can no longer be valid. A monitoring job checks many streamed responses for structural problems. It must keep up with long responses split into thousands of tiny chunks, so it cannot re-read everything it has seen each time a chunk arrives.
sections.problem: Implement json_stream_status(streams). streams is a list of streamed responses, each a list of text chunks in arrival order (a chunk may be empty). Return one result per stream, in order, by this exercise's structural rules. Whitespace is space, tab, newline and carriage return. Leading whitespace is skipped; the first other character must be { or [, or the stream is invalid at that character. Outside strings, { and [ open a bracket, and } or ] must close the most recently opened bracket of the same kind, or it is invalid. " starts a string; inside a string, " ends it, a backslash escapes the next character (so \" does not end the string and \\ is one backslash), and brackets are just text. Every other character outside strings is accepted: this check covers structure, not values. The response is complete when the bracket that opened it closes. Return ("complete", k) with k the 0-based index of the chunk holding that closing bracket; ("invalid", i) with i the 0-based position of the first invalid character in the stream's text (all chunks joined); or ("incomplete", n) when the stream ends first, with n the number of brackets still open (0 if none was opened). {{escape_rule}} {{control_rule}}
sections.constraints: Streams can be hundreds of thousands of characters, in chunks of 1 to 4 characters, in the timing check. Re-scanning the accumulated text after every chunk is quadratic and too slow; keep a scanner state per stream so every character is read once.
sections.assumptions: Responses and chunk boundaries are synthetic; the structural rules are this exercise's, a subset of JSON (numbers, literals, commas and colons are not checked). Text is ASCII. What the response says is never inspected, only its structure.
sections.criteria: One pass with a per-stream state; a bracket stack that rejects mismatches at the right position; strings and escapes honoured across chunk boundaries; chunk index of completion and character position of the first invalid character; incomplete with the open-bracket count; at Hard, JSON's escapes only, four hex digits after \u, and nothing but whitespace after completion; at Very Hard, raw control characters in strings rejected and escapes split across chunks; O(total characters) with a clear argument; good answers on full JSON, early emission and UTF-8.

clarifications.q: Does a } inside a string close anything?
clarifications.a: No. Inside a string only " (unescaped) and the backslash matter.

clarifications.q: A chunk ends with a backslash.
clarifications.a: The escape continues into the next chunk; the next character, wherever it arrives, is the escaped one.

clarifications.q: How do I count positions with empty chunks?
clarifications.a: Positions are in the joined text, so empty chunks add nothing; chunk indexes still count them.

clarifications.q: The stream is only whitespace so far.
clarifications.a: ("incomplete", 0).

clarifications.q: Can I raise on bad input?
clarifications.a: No. Return the tuple; an invalid stream is a normal result.

hints: The state you need between chunks is small: the stack of open brackets, whether you are inside a string, whether the last character was an unescaped backslash, and whether the response has started or finished.
Process each character once, chunk by chunk, keeping a running position; record the chunk index at the moment the stack becomes empty.
Check \\" and "\\" by hand: whether a quote ends a string depends on the escape state, not on whether the previous character is a backslash.
followups: Extend the scanner to check full JSON: commas, colons, numbers and true/false/null. Which states do you add?
The client also wants the value of a top-level key as soon as it is complete, before the rest of the object arrives. How would you emit it?
Responses are UTF-8 bytes, and a chunk can end in the middle of a multi-byte character. What changes?
A monitoring job reads 50 000 concurrent streams. How much state per stream do you keep, and when can you drop it?

rules.ask: You call json.loads on the accumulated text after each chunk. How many characters does that read for a 150 000-character response in 60 000 chunks?
What does your check say about the string "a\\" followed by a quote? Is the quote escaped?
Joining is fine once. Where does your code join or re-scan, and how often does that happen per stream?
Counting brackets accepts {[}]. How does your scanner reject it, and at which position?
Can a regular expression match balanced nested brackets? What would you keep instead between chunks?

templates.title: Adapter slots on a dedicated endpoint: least-frequently-used eviction with a recency tie-break
templates.subtopic: LFU in O(1): frequency buckets of insertion-ordered dicts, recency tie-break, counts reset on eviction

sections.scenario: A customer fine-tuned many LoRA adapters from the same base model and serves them all on one dedicated endpoint running {{base_model}}. The endpoint can hold only a fixed number of adapters loaded at once, called slots here. A request for an adapter that is already loaded is served straight away; a request for one that is not has to wait while it is loaded, and when every slot is taken another adapter is evicted first. The customer wants to replay their own request log against a slot count and see the hits, the misses and the evictions in order, before choosing how many slots to pay for. The eviction rule is this exercise's rule; check current docs for how real endpoints load and unload adapters.
sections.problem: Implement adapter_cache(slots, requests, pinned=()). Process requests in order. A request for a loaded adapter is a hit: its use count goes up by 1 and it becomes the most recently used. A request for an adapter that is not loaded is a miss: if fewer than slots adapters are loaded it is loaded with a use count of 1; otherwise the loaded adapter with the lowest use count is evicted first, ties broken by least recent use (the adapter whose latest request, hit or load, came earliest), and then the new one is loaded with a count of 1. An evicted adapter's count is forgotten: if it is requested again, it is a miss and starts again at 1. Return (hits, misses, evictions), where evictions is the list of evicted adapter ids in the order they were evicted. {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check replays 150 000 requests on an endpoint with 4 000 to 6 000 slots, tens of thousands of distinct adapters and tens of thousands of misses. Scanning every slot for the victim on each miss is hundreds of millions of steps in CPython. Constant or logarithmic time per request is expected.
sections.assumptions: Slot counts, adapter names and traffic are hypothetical. Every adapter is the same size, so one adapter takes one slot. Loading time is not modelled: only which requests hit or miss. Adapter ids are compared exactly as strings.
sections.criteria: Hits and misses counted correctly, with the loading request a miss; the lowest count evicted, ties by least recent use; counts forgotten on eviction; evictions listed in order; at Hard, base-model requests ignored and zero slots handled; at Very Hard, pinned adapters never evicted and misses served without loading when nothing can be evicted; O(1) per request with count groups (or O(log slots) with a heap and lazy deletion, argued carefully); a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on ageing, sizes and choosing the slot count.

clarifications.q: Does the request that loads an adapter count as a use?
clarifications.a: Yes. After the load its count is 1 and it is the most recently used adapter. The request itself is a miss, not a hit.

clarifications.q: Which adapter goes when two have the same lowest count?
clarifications.a: The one used least recently, where "used" means its latest request, hit or load.

clarifications.q: Does an adapter keep its count after it is evicted?
clarifications.a: No. It is forgotten, and the adapter starts again at 1 if it comes back.

clarifications.q: Is the order of evictions the order of the misses that caused them?
clarifications.a: Yes. One eviction at most per miss.

clarifications.q: Is the request log sorted by adapter or by time?
clarifications.a: By arrival time only. Process it in the order given.

hints: Group the loaded adapters by use count. The victim is in the group with the smallest count, and within it, the one used least recently.
A hit moves an adapter from group f to the end of group f + 1. So the order inside every group is simply the order in which adapters arrived in it, which is their order of last use.
Keep the smallest non-empty count in a variable. A load sets it to 1; a hit that empties group f while it was the smallest moves it to f + 1. It never needs a search.
followups: Use counts never fade: an adapter that was busy last week can keep a slot forever. How would you age the counts, and what does each option cost per request?
Adapters now differ in size by LoRA rank, and a large one takes several slots and longer to load. How does the eviction rule change?
The endpoint runs several replicas, each with its own slots. How would you route requests so that each adapter stays loaded on as few replicas as possible without overloading one?
The customer wants the smallest slot count that keeps misses under 2% over a week of traffic. How would you find it, and what must you check before you binary search over slot counts?

rules.ask: How many slots does each miss look at in the timing check, and how many misses are there? Multiply them.
After a hit, the adapter's old entry is still in the heap. How do you recognise a stale entry when it reaches the top, and how large can the heap grow?
Which order does each group keep, and why is it the same as least-recent use among adapters with that count?
When exactly does the smallest count change? Show the case where a hit changes it.
Give a request sequence where least-recently-used and this rule evict different adapters, and say which one the customer would prefer.

templates.title: Per-tenant latency questions: how many requests were slower than a threshold
templates.subtopic: sorting queries by threshold, a Fenwick tree over time per tenant, half-open ranges

sections.scenario: Serverless inference serves many open models to many tenants on shared capacity, and each tenant can see its own latency. A latency report built for each tenant asks many questions of the same form: how many of this tenant's requests in this time range had {{metric}} slower than this threshold? A report run asks tens of thousands of them at once, over different tenants, ranges and thresholds, against one day of request records. Each answer counts only the asking tenant's own requests; other tenants appear in nothing a tenant sees.
sections.problem: Implement slow_request_counts(requests, queries). requests is a list of (tenant, ts, latency_ms, model) in no particular order, where ts is an integer timestamp and latency_ms an integer. queries is a list of (tenant, t_from, t_to, threshold_ms, model). For each query, return the number of requests of that tenant with t_from <= ts < t_to and latency_ms > threshold_ms (strictly slower), in the order the queries were given. When model is None, requests to every model count. A tenant with no requests gets 0. {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check has 120 000 to 150 000 requests and 30 000 queries over three to five tenants, and most queries cover more than half of the day, so a query's slice of its tenant's requests holds tens of thousands of rows. Scanning that slice for every query is about a billion comparisons. Something close to O((n + q) log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Tenants, models, timestamps and latencies are hypothetical; how real latency is measured and reported is not described here, so check current docs. All queries are known before you answer any of them. Timestamps can repeat.
sections.criteria: Half-open time ranges, strictly slower latencies, only the asking tenant's requests, answers in query order and 0 for unknown tenants; at Hard, failed requests never counted and malformed ranges answered -1; at Very Hard, model filters honoured with None meaning all models; an offline method in O((n + q) log n) (or an online merge-sort or wavelet tree in O(log² n) per query, argued carefully); a clear explanation of why processing queries by threshold works; sensible answers on online queries, percentiles and low volume.

clarifications.q: Is a request exactly at t_to inside the range?
clarifications.a: No. t_from is inclusive and t_to exclusive.

clarifications.q: Does a latency equal to the threshold count?
clarifications.a: No. Only strictly slower requests count.

clarifications.q: Do I have to answer the queries in order?
clarifications.a: You must return the answers in the order the queries were given, but you may compute them in any order.

clarifications.q: Can two requests have the same timestamp?
clarifications.a: Yes, and both count.

clarifications.q: Can a query name a tenant that sent nothing?
clarifications.a: Yes. The answer is 0.

hints: Each answer has two conditions: time inside a range, and latency above a threshold. With only the time condition, a sorted list of timestamps and two bisects would do. What stops that here?
Answer the queries in decreasing order of threshold. Before each one, add every request slower than its threshold that has not been added yet. Requests only ever get added.
Then each query asks "how many added requests of this tenant have a time in [t_from, t_to)?". A Fenwick tree over the tenant's timestamps in sorted order answers that with two prefix sums.
followups: Queries now arrive one at a time from a live dashboard, so you cannot sort them first. Which structure answers each one quickly, and what does it cost in memory?
The report wants the 95th percentile of each tenant's latency per range instead of a count. How would you get it from the same kind of structure?
A tenant has only 14 requests in a range. What should the report show, and what must it not claim?
Requests keep arriving during the day and the report is re-run every five minutes. What would you keep between runs instead of starting again?

rules.ask: After bisecting to the time range, how many requests are in a typical slice in the timing check, and what do you then do with each of them?
What does your tree index by, in what order do requests enter it, and why does that order make each answer correct?
That structure answers online. What does it cost per query and in memory at 150 000 requests, and when would you still prefer sorting the queries?
A vectorised scan is fast per element, but how many elements does each query still touch, and how does that grow with the number of queries?
How would your structure turn "how many are slower than x" into "what is the 95th percentile", and how many steps does that take?

templates.title: Debug the fine-tuning dataset validator
templates.subtopic: JSON Lines, 1-based line numbers, role order, token limits, repeated keys

sections.scenario: Customers upload training files for fine-tuning in a conversational JSON Lines format: each line is one example, a JSON object whose messages list holds turns with a role and a content. Before a job is queued, the platform validates the file and reports problems by line number and error code. The validator never shows, stores or summarises the content of a line: the customer asked for a format check, and that is all it does. Customers have reported several problems. Errors point at the wrong line in files with blank lines. A file with a system turn in the middle of a conversation passed validation and the job then failed. Examples over the length limit passed when they had a long system turn. An assistant answer made only of spaces passed as if it were text. A line with several repeated keys got the same error many times. The validator below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix validate_dataset(lines, max_tokens) so that it meets this specification. The format and every rule here are this exercise's rules; check current docs for the real format. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Lines. lines[0] is line 1 of the file. Lines that are empty or only whitespace are skipped, but they still count in the numbering. If every line is blank (or there are none), return [(0, "no_examples")].
  2. JSON. A line that is not valid JSON gets invalid_json, and nothing else is checked on it.
  3. Repeated keys. If any JSON object on the line (the line itself or any object inside it) repeats a key, the line gets duplicate_key, once however many keys repeat. A repeated key's last value is the one that counts.
  4. Messages. The line must be an object with a non-empty list under messages; otherwise it gets missing_messages, and the checks below are skipped. Every message is an object with a string role and a string content.
  5. Role order. An optional system turn first, then turns alternating user, assistant, starting with user and ending with assistant. Anything else gets bad_role_order: a system turn anywhere else, two turns in a row with the same role, an unknown role, or a conversation with no user turn.
  6. Empty answers. If any assistant turn has content that is empty or only whitespace, the line gets empty_assistant (once).
  7. Length. The line's token count is the number of whitespace-separated words (len(content.split())) summed over every turn, the system turn included. Over max_tokens gets too_long; exactly max_tokens is allowed.
  8. Output. A list of (line_number, code), by line number, and within a line in the order duplicate_key, missing_messages, bad_role_order, empty_assistant, too_long. A valid file returns [].
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. Report codes and line numbers only, never any content. Up to 100 000 lines, processed in close to linear time.
sections.assumptions: The format, the error codes, the word-count token rule and the limits are hypothetical; real fine-tuning formats and token counts (which use the model's tokenizer) differ, so check current docs. Line contents are synthetic placeholder words. Messages inside a parsed messages list are always objects with string role and content in this exercise.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its customer symptom; line numbers counted over the whole file, blank lines included; a system turn accepted only first; every turn counted toward the limit; whitespace-only answers rejected; repeated keys reported once per line; minimal fixes that keep the output format; no content ever in the output; a regression test per bug.

clarifications.q: Do blank lines count in the line numbers?
clarifications.a: Yes. They are skipped for checking, but line 5 is the fifth line of the file whatever comes before it.

clarifications.q: Is a conversation with only a system turn valid?
clarifications.a: No. It has no user turn, so it gets bad_role_order.

clarifications.q: Does the system turn count toward the length?
clarifications.a: Yes. The limit is over every turn.

clarifications.q: If messages appears twice, which one is checked?
clarifications.a: The last one, as the JSON parser keeps it. The line also gets duplicate_key.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Feed the validator a file whose second line is blank and whose third line is broken, and read the line number it reports.
Which turns does turns hold, and where else in the function is it used?
What does " ".strip() return, and what does the empty-answer check compare against?
Count how many times duplicate_key can be appended for one line.
followups: A customer's file has 2 million lines and 40 000 errors. What do you return to them, and what do you keep?
The real limit is in model tokens, not words, and each base model has its own tokenizer. Where does tokenization happen, and how do you keep it fast on large files?
The customer asks why a line was rejected, and support may not open the file. What can the error report say, and what should it never say?
Validation runs on upload, and the job starts hours later on a different base model with a smaller limit. How do you keep the two consistent?

rules.ask: Where does the line number come from in your fix, and which test would have caught the original mistake?
How does your fix treat a system turn in the middle, and two system turns at the start?
Which other check in the function depends on how whitespace is treated, and is it consistent with this one?
Repeated keys can be inside a message, not only at the top level. How does your fix see those, and how many times does it report them?
The word rule here is a stand-in. What changes in cost and in correctness when the count uses the model's real tokenizer?

templates.title: Fine-tuning job pipeline: from uploaded dataset to a deployable model
templates.subtopic: validation, queueing, checkpointing, job state machines and customer-visible events

sections.scenario: A cloud for open models lets customers fine-tune any of {{base_models}} base models. A customer uploads a training file of up to {{max_dataset_gb}} GB, chooses a LoRA or a full fine-tune and its settings, and starts a job. The job waits in a queue for capacity, trains, saves up to {{checkpoints}} checkpoints along the way, and ends with a model the customer can deploy to an endpoint or download. About {{daily_jobs}} jobs start each day. Customers watch their jobs through a status page and an API that list the job's state and events, and they can cancel at any time.
sections.problem: Design the fine-tuning job pipeline. Cover the upload and the validation the customer asked for (format, lengths, counts, never content), the job's state machine and its events, the queue and how jobs are admitted to capacity, how training is checkpointed and resumed after a failure, how cancellation works at every stage, how the finished model is registered and made ready to deploy, and what the customer sees at each step.
sections.constraints: A job's state shown to the customer must never go backwards or skip a failure. A training failure must resume from the last checkpoint rather than start again. A cancelled job must stop consuming paid capacity within minutes. Validation must finish before a job uses training capacity, and must report problems by line and code without exposing content. Customer files, checkpoints and models are isolated per customer.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, file sizes, checkpoint counts and the number of base models are hypothetical; how real fine-tuning jobs are scheduled, priced or checkpointed is not described here, so check current docs. Training runs on capacity you do not need to design. Every job has a stable id.
sections.criteria: Files and validation separated from jobs, with validation reporting lines and codes only; a written state machine with idempotent, sequenced events that never move backwards; fair admission from the queue; durable, verified checkpoints and resume from the last one; cancellation honoured at every stage, including the handover; a registered, deployable model; per-customer isolation; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is validation part of the job, or a separate step?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but the customer must see validation errors before the job is queued, and a file that passed validation should not be re-validated for every job that uses it.

clarifications.q: Can a customer change settings after starting?
clarifications.a: No. They cancel and start a new job; the new job can reuse the same uploaded file.

clarifications.q: What does the customer get at the end?
clarifications.a: A model id they can deploy, plus the checkpoints they asked to keep. For a LoRA job, that is an adapter on top of the base model.

clarifications.q: Are failed jobs charged?
clarifications.a: This exercise's rule: training time is charged only for work that ends in a usable checkpoint or model. Say how you record it.

hints: Separate files from jobs: an uploaded file has its own validation state and can serve many jobs.
Write the job's state machine down first, with every allowed transition, including cancelled and failed from each state, and make every transition an event with a sequence number.
Treat a checkpoint as a durable, registered artefact with its own id: resuming is "start from checkpoint k", and the final model is just the last checkpoint promoted.
followups: A base model is deprecated while jobs on it are queued. What happens to them, and what do customers see?
A customer re-runs the same job on the same file with the same seed and gets a different loss curve. What would you have recorded to explain it?
Queue waits grow to hours for the largest base models. How would you show an honest estimate, and how would you decide admission order?
At {{daily_jobs}} jobs a day, which part of the pipeline breaks first, and how do you scale it?

rules.ask: A "training started" event arrives after "cancelled" for the same job. What does your state machine do, and what is charged?
Training fails just after a checkpoint is written but before it is registered. Does the resume use it, and how do you know it is complete?
One customer starts 300 jobs in a minute. How does your queue keep other customers' jobs moving?
What exactly does validation read, and how do you prove to the customer that nothing else read their file?
A job has failed three times on the same step. When do you stop retrying, and what do you tell the customer?

incidents: A storage hiccup makes some checkpoint writes look successful while the files are incomplete, and resumed jobs crash at load for several hours.
A customer uploads a {{max_dataset_gb}} GB file, validation takes longer than the upload, and the status page shows "queued" the whole time.
Cancellations during the queued-to-training handover are lost, and a few cancelled jobs train for an hour and are charged.

templates.title: Multi-model serverless metering: request events to daily per-tenant usage
templates.subtopic: per-model tokenizers, versioned prices, late and duplicate events, invoice reconciliation

sections.scenario: Serverless inference offers {{models}} open models behind one API, served by about {{model_servers}} model servers, and tenants pay per token by model: input and output tokens priced separately, with prices that change over time as models are added, upgraded and repriced. Each model counts tokens with its own tokenizer. About {{daily_requests}} requests a day produce usage events. Most events arrive within seconds, but a server that loses its connection can deliver them up to {{late_hours}} hours late, and retries can deliver the same event twice. Tenants want their usage per model per day the next morning, and finance needs it to match the invoice exactly.
sections.problem: Design the metering pipeline from model-server usage events to daily per-tenant, per-model usage and charges. Cover the usage event and where token counts come from, how events are collected and deduplicated, how late events reach the right day, how the price in force for each request is found and stored, how a day becomes final and how corrections are issued, how the numbers a tenant sees match the invoice, and how each tenant sees only its own usage.
sections.constraints: An event delivered twice must never be charged twice. Late events up to {{late_hours}} hours must land on the day the request happened. Every charge must be reproducible later from stored events and the price version used. A price change takes effect at a stated instant, never "whenever the pipeline notices". Prompt and completion contents never enter the metering pipeline: only counts, ids and timestamps.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, model counts, server counts, lateness and every price rule are hypothetical; check current docs for real pricing and metering. Each request has a unique id. Servers timestamp events with their own clocks, which can drift by seconds.
sections.criteria: Request id as event identity, with duplicates dropped where it can be proven; event-time days with late events rebuilding their day; token counts with a stated source and tokenizer version; versioned prices with exact effective instants, stored with each charge; finality and versioned corrections; tenant numbers equal to the invoice; per-tenant isolation and no content in the pipeline; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Who counts the tokens: the API layer or the model server?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but say which and why; the two can disagree when a request is cut off mid-stream.

clarifications.q: Which time decides the price: when the request started, or when it finished?
clarifications.a: This exercise's rule: when the request was received. Store it with the event.

clarifications.q: Are failed requests charged?
clarifications.a: This exercise's rule: input tokens are charged only if the model produced output; a request that failed before any output is free. Keep the status in the event.

clarifications.q: Can a request use a fine-tuned adapter on serverless?
clarifications.a: Assume not in this exercise; dedicated endpoints are billed separately per replica-minute.

hints: Make the request id the identity of a usage event, so a duplicate is the same row, not a second one.
Store the tokenizer version and the price version with each priced event; a reprice is then a new version, never an edit.
Build daily totals as partitions you can rebuild, keyed by the request's day in UTC, and let late events trigger a rebuild of their day.
followups: A model's tokenizer is fixed in a new version and counts 3% fewer tokens for the same text. Which past charges change, and what do you tell tenants?
A price cut is announced at noon and backdated to the start of the day. How do the day's totals change, and how is the invoice corrected?
A tenant says their own client-side count is 5% lower than yours. How do you investigate without reading their prompts?
Volume grows ten times past {{daily_requests}} requests a day. Which stage breaks first?

rules.ask: Where exactly is a duplicate event dropped, and what would prove to finance that it was?
An event from 23:58 arrives at 01:30. Which day is it charged to, and when is the earlier day final?
A batch of events is replayed after a crash halfway through. How do your counters avoid counting part of it twice?
Two price rows overlap by a minute after a rushed change. Which one wins, and how would you have prevented it?
The API layer and the model server count different tokens for a request cut off mid-stream. Which one is charged, and why?

incidents: One model server restarts with its clock a day behind, and its events land on the previous day for every tenant it served.
A retry storm after a network partition delivers some events three times, and one tenant's usage page shows triple usage for an hour.
A price change is deployed to the pricing table before its announced start time, and requests in between are charged the new price.

templates.title: Fine-tuning jobs as data — uploaded datasets, validation results, LoRA or full configs, states, checkpoints and the model each job produced
templates.subtopic: immutable inputs, validation results without content, method subtypes, job state history, artefact lineage

sections.scenario: A cloud for open models lets customers fine-tune an open base model on their own data. In this exercise's model a customer uploads a dataset file (up to {{max_dataset_size}}, in a line-per-example format), the platform validates it as the customer asked (format, roles, lengths by a stated token rule), and the customer starts a job: a base model version, a method (a LoRA fine-tune with a rank and other adapter settings, or a full fine-tune), hyperparameters, and optionally a validation file. A job waits in a queue, runs, saves about {{checkpoints_per_job}} checkpoints, and ends completed, failed or cancelled; a completed job produces a model (an adapter or full weights) that the customer can deploy. Jobs can be retried after an infrastructure failure. There are about {{jobs_per_day}} jobs a day; checkpoints that are not the final model are kept for {{retention_days}} days (this exercise's rule). Customers see their own jobs, events and models; the platform needs outcome rates by base model and method, time queued, and where jobs fail.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: uploaded files and their identity; validation runs and their results, stored without keeping any example's content; job configurations, with the LoRA and full methods modelled so that each has only the settings that apply to it; job states over time and retries; checkpoints; and the produced model, with its lineage back to the job, the checkpoint, the base model version and the exact dataset file. Show how to answer: "jobs completed, failed at validation, failed in training and cancelled, per base model and method, per week"; "minutes queued per job attempt"; "which dataset file, base model version and checkpoint produced this deployed model"; and "files whose validation failed, by error code and validator version".
sections.constraints: An uploaded file is never changed; a customer who fixes a dataset uploads a new file. Validation results hold counts, line numbers, error codes and token totals only, never text from the file. A job's configuration is fixed once it is submitted. A produced model must stay traceable to its inputs for as long as it can be deployed, even after checkpoints expire. A customer sees only its own files, jobs and models.
sections.assumptions: Job volumes, checkpoint counts, retention periods, file sizes, state names and the token rule are hypothetical; check current docs for any real fine-tuning product's formats and limits. Training internals (hardware, schedulers) are out of scope; a job reports its state changes and checkpoints as events.
sections.criteria: Files immutable and identified by checksum; validation runs versioned, with results as counts, line numbers and error codes, never content; job configurations immutable with method-specific settings typed per method; job attempts and state events with derived queue and run times; checkpoints and the produced model with lineage to file, base model version, job and checkpoint that survives expiry and deletion; customer-level access; volumes and retention reasoned at the stated scale; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a job be retried?
clarifications.a: Yes, after an infrastructure failure the platform retries it as another attempt of the same job. The customer sees one job; operations need every attempt.

clarifications.q: Does the validator change?
clarifications.a: Yes. It is versioned, and a new version may accept or reject things the old one did not. A file can be validated more than once.

clarifications.q: Which settings does each method have?
clarifications.a: In this exercise a LoRA job has a rank, an alpha, target module groups and a dropout; a full fine-tune has none of those. Both have epochs, a learning rate and a batch size.

clarifications.q: Can the customer delete a file after a job used it?
clarifications.a: Yes. The file's contents go; the model's lineage must still say which file (by id and checksum) it was trained on.

clarifications.q: Is the final model one of the checkpoints?
clarifications.a: Your choice; state it. In this exercise the produced model is promoted from one checkpoint and kept while the customer keeps it.

hints: Separate the immutable inputs (file, by checksum; job configuration) from what happens to them (validation runs, job attempts, state events).
Method settings belong in a subtype per method (or a typed column group with checks), not in one wide table full of NULLs or an unvalidated blob.
A state history as events per attempt gives queue time, run time and failure stage without overwriting anything.
followups: Walk one job through upload, a failed validation, a new file, a passing validation, queueing, a node failure, a retry, three checkpoints and completion. Which rows exist at the end?
The validator gets a new version that rejects a format the old one accepted. Which reports change, and how does the customer see why an earlier job ran on that file?
A customer deletes the dataset file and asks which models were trained on it. Answer from your model without the contents.

At {{jobs_per_day}} jobs a day with {{checkpoints_per_job}} checkpoints each and {{retention_days}}-day retention, estimate the rows and the artefact bytes you track, and say what you partition or expire.

rules.ask: Analysts ask for completion rates by LoRA rank. How do they query a rank stored inside a blob, and what stops a full fine-tune from carrying a rank?
A job was retried after a node failure. With one status column updated in place, how do you report minutes queued for the first attempt?
A customer uploads a corrected file with the same name. Which file did last week's job train on, and how does your model know?
The validation report needs to say what is wrong without keeping the customer's text. What exactly do you store per error?
Checkpoints expire after {{retention_days}} days. What happens to the lineage of a model promoted from one of them?

incidents: A validator upgrade began rejecting files with a trailing empty line. Validation results were stored as one row per file, overwritten on each run, so a customer whose job had trained successfully a month earlier now saw that same file marked failed, and support could not explain which validator had passed it.

A retried job reused its attempt row: the retry overwrote the first attempt's start time. At about {{jobs_per_day}} jobs a day the weekly time-in-queue report quietly dropped every first attempt, and the retry rate looked like zero.

Checkpoints expired after {{retention_days}} days, and the produced model's record pointed only at the checkpoint's storage path. A customer redeploying a model trained more than {{retention_days}} days earlier got a missing-file error, and nobody could say which checkpoint it had been.

templates.title: LoRA adapters and dedicated endpoints as data — endpoints, replicas, base models, adapters attached over time, and the adapter that served each request
templates.subtopic: configuration versions, replica intervals, attachment intervals, compatibility constraints, request attribution

sections.scenario: A customer of a cloud for open models runs a dedicated endpoint: one base model version served on replicas the customer pays for by the minute while each replica runs (this exercise's rule). The endpoint scales between a minimum and a maximum of up to {{max_replicas}} replicas. Several LoRA adapters, up to {{max_adapters}} per endpoint, can be attached to the same endpoint, so one deployment serves many fine-tuned variants; a request names an adapter or asks for the base model alone. Customers attach and detach adapters, upload new adapter versions, change scaling settings, and sometimes move an endpoint to a newer base model version. There are about {{endpoints}} dedicated endpoints and {{requests_per_day}} requests a day across them. The customer wants per-adapter traffic and latency and an explainable bill; the platform needs replica-minutes and the adapters attached at any moment.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: endpoints and their configuration over time (base model version, scaling bounds, hardware class described generally); replicas as intervals from start to stop, with the minutes billed per replica; adapters, their versions and the base model version each was trained for; attachments of adapter versions to endpoints over time; and request records that say which endpoint, replica, adapter version (or none) served them. Show how to answer: "replica-minutes per endpoint and day"; "requests, tokens and median time to first token per adapter version and day"; "the adapters attached to this endpoint at 14:00 last Tuesday"; and "requests that named an adapter not attached at the time".
sections.constraints: An adapter can only be attached to an endpoint serving the base model version it was trained for. Configuration changes never overwrite history. A replica-minute is billed for each started minute a replica runs (this exercise's rule; check current docs). A customer sees only its own endpoints, adapters and requests.
sections.assumptions: Endpoint counts, replica bounds, adapter limits, volumes and the billing rule are hypothetical; check current docs for any real dedicated-endpoint product. Loading an adapter into a replica's memory is an operational event you may model, but this template is about the records, not the serving algorithm.
sections.criteria: Endpoint configuration versioned; replicas as intervals with the billing rule applied per interval; adapters and adapter versions separate, each tied to its base model version; attachments as intervals with the compatibility rule enforced; requests that record the resolved adapter version and replica; replica-minutes, per-adapter metrics and as-of attachment queries defined on stated grains; storage and rollups reasoned at the stated volumes; customer-level access; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does a request name an adapter by id or by name?
clarifications.a: By a customer-chosen name. A name can later point at a newer upload of the adapter.

clarifications.q: What happens to attached adapters when the endpoint moves to a newer base model version?
clarifications.a: Adapters trained for the old version cannot stay attached. In this exercise the change detaches them, and the customer re-attaches compatible versions.

clarifications.q: Are replica start and stop times exact?
clarifications.a: They come from scale events that can arrive late or, rarely, twice.

clarifications.q: Is a request to the base model alone billed differently?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; tokens and replica-minutes are the same. Customers still want to see the split.

clarifications.q: Can two adapters share a name at once on one endpoint?
clarifications.a: No. A name is unique per endpoint at any moment.

hints: Treat the endpoint, the adapter and the adapter version as identities; their settings and attachments are intervals with a start and an end.
Resolve the adapter name to an adapter version at request time and store the version on the request record, not only the name.
Replica-minutes come from replica intervals clipped to the day; the billing rule applies per replica interval, not per endpoint.
followups: A customer uploads a new version of an adapter under the same name while traffic flows. Show the attachment rows before and after, and which version each request records.
The endpoint moves to a newer base model version. Which rows change, which are closed, and how do yesterday's per-adapter reports stay right?
A replica's stop event arrives twice, and another's never arrives. How does your model keep replica-minutes right, and what does the customer see on the bill in the meantime?
At {{requests_per_day}} requests a day over {{endpoints}} endpoints, what do you keep at request grain, what do you roll up, and how quickly can "requests per adapter version per hour" be answered?

rules.ask: The customer re-uploaded the adapter under the same name at noon. Which version served the 11:59 requests, and can your records tell?
Support asks which adapters were attached at 14:00 last Tuesday. How does a current flag answer that?
The endpoint scaled from two replicas to five and back within an hour. How do you bill per minute per running replica from a count?
The endpoint moved to a newer base model version. What stops an adapter trained for the old version from staying attached in your model?
A replica ran from 10:00:30 to 10:02:10. How many minutes does this exercise's rule bill, and where does your model apply it?

incidents: A customer re-uploaded an adapter under the same name. Requests stored only the name, so the per-adapter latency report merged two versions and showed a regression that belonged to neither; with up to {{max_adapters}} adapters per endpoint, support could not say which version had served the slow requests.

An endpoint was moved to a newer base model version by updating its configuration row. Adapters trained for the old version stayed attached in the records, and requests that named them failed while the console said they were live.
A scale-down event for one of {{max_replicas}} replicas was lost. The replica interval stayed open, and the customer's bill showed replica-minutes for a replica that had stopped two days earlier.

templates.title: The open-model catalogue as data — families, versions, licences, context lengths, serverless or dedicated availability, deprecations and named replacements
templates.subtopic: reference data with history, licence versions, offerings per deployment type, versioned notices, catalogue as of a date

sections.scenario: A cloud for open models keeps a public catalogue of the open models it serves. In this exercise's model a model family (from one publisher) has versions; a version has a parameter count, a context length the weights support, a licence, and offerings: available on serverless inference, on dedicated endpoints, or both, each with its own context length limit and token prices (hypothetical). About {{new_per_week}} new versions are added a week; the catalogue holds about {{catalogue_models}} versions across about {{licence_kinds}} licence kinds. Versions are deprecated with at least {{notice_days}} days' notice (this exercise's rule; check current docs), and a deprecation names a replacement. Publishers sometimes change a licence; notices are sometimes postponed. The catalogue page, the API's model list, billing and compliance reporting all read the catalogue, and they must agree about any date.
sections.problem: Design the data model for the catalogue. Cover: families, publishers and versions, and the identifier the API uses for a version; licences as versioned documents with the properties reporting needs (for example, commercial use allowed, attribution required), and which licence applied to a version over time; offerings per deployment type with context length limits and prices over time; availability windows; and deprecation notices with announcement time, deprecation date and the named replacement, including notices that are later revised. Show how to answer: "the catalogue as the API listed it on a past date"; "serverless versions deprecating in the next 30 days, with their replacements"; "versions whose licence changed after a tenant first called them"; and "the context length and price that applied to a request at its time".
sections.constraints: Nothing in the catalogue is overwritten; any past listing can be reproduced exactly. A version's identifier never points at different weights. Prices are integer minor units per token count with a currency, applying from their effective time. A replacement must be a version in the catalogue. Tenants appear only in aggregate, except a tenant's own usage shown to that tenant.
sections.assumptions: Catalogue sizes, rates, notice periods, licence kinds, prices and context limits are hypothetical; check current docs for any real catalogue, licence or deprecation policy. Licence text is stored and referenced, not interpreted by this model; legal judgement is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Identity separated from changing facts, each with history; licences as versioned entities with reportable properties and version-to-licence intervals; offerings per deployment type with context limits and integer-minor-unit prices over time; deprecation notices as immutable announcements with dates and replacements, revisions kept; the catalogue reproducible as of any date; a go-live check that offerings are complete; tenant data aggregated or scoped to the tenant; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can serverless and dedicated offer different context lengths for the same version?
clarifications.a: Yes, in this exercise. The serverless offering may cap context below what the weights support.

clarifications.q: What if the publisher changes the licence of an existing version?
clarifications.a: A new licence applies from a stated time. Requests before that time were served under the old one, and compliance needs to see both.

clarifications.q: Can a deprecation notice change?
clarifications.a: Yes. A later notice can postpone the date or name a different replacement; earlier notices stay on record because tenants were told them.

clarifications.q: Is a version ever re-published with different weights under the same identifier?
clarifications.a: Never in this exercise. Different weights are a new version.

clarifications.q: Does the catalogue hold usage?
clarifications.a: No. Usage lives in request records; the catalogue is what they join to.

hints: Separate identity (family, version) from facts that change (licence assignment, offerings, prices, availability, notices), each with an effective range or an announcement time.
Model licences as their own versioned table, and the version-to-licence link as intervals; properties used in reporting are columns on the licence version, not free text.
"As listed on date D" is a set of as-of lookups on each history table; make every one of them answerable the same way.
followups: Write the query shape for "the catalogue as the API listed it on a past date", including offerings, context lengths, prices and deprecation status.

A publisher changes a version's licence to one that forbids a use some tenants rely on. Which records change, and how do you list the tenants who called the version since the change, without exposing any tenant to another?
A deprecation is postponed and its replacement changed. Which notices exist afterwards, and which date does the migration report judge last month's calls by?
With {{new_per_week}} versions added a week and a {{notice_days}}-day notice period, sketch how the catalogue page, the API list and billing stay consistent when a new version goes live.

rules.ask: The publisher changed the licence on the 10th. Compliance asks which licence applied to calls on the 9th. Can a single column on the version answer that?
Serverless caps context below what the weights support. Which context length does the request validator use, and where does each one live in your model?
The deprecation was postponed after tenants were notified. Which date did tenants hear first, and can your model show both?
A name that means "the latest version" moves to new weights. How does a request record stay reproducible when the name moves?
A price changes at midnight UTC while requests are in flight. Which price applies to a request that started at 23:59:58, and how does your model decide?

incidents: A publisher's licence change was applied by editing the licence column on the version. The compliance export for the previous quarter now showed the new licence for every call, including calls made months before the change.

A deprecation was postponed by editing the existing notice's date. Tenants had been told the original date {{notice_days}} days earlier; the migration report judged their calls by the new date, and a tenant's account review started from figures that contradicted the notice they had received.

A new version went live on the catalogue page before its serverless offering had prices. With about {{new_per_week}} versions added a week, the billing pipeline priced a day of that version's calls at zero before anyone noticed.

templates.title: Inference requests as data — serverless or dedicated, model version, adapter, tenant, queue time, time to first token, generation time and token counts
templates.subtopic: request fact grain, attempts, latency decomposition, token counts per tokenizer, mergeable latency rollups, no content stored

sections.scenario: A cloud for open models serves requests on shared serverless models and on customers' dedicated endpoints, with or without a LoRA adapter. In this exercise's model each request passes through a router, waits in a queue, is processed by a model server, and returns tokens; about {{streaming_share}} of requests stream their output. Every stage reports timings, and the model server reports token counts by the model version's own tokenizer. There are about {{requests_per_day}} requests a day from about {{tenants}} tenants. Request-level records are kept for {{raw_retention_days}} days (this exercise's rule); prompts and outputs are never stored in these records. Tenants see their own latency and token usage; the platform needs latency by model version, deployment type and stage, and tokens per tenant that agree with usage reporting.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: the grain of the request fact and how retries and client cancellations appear; the timestamps you keep and the durations you derive (queue time, time to first token, generation time, end-to-end), with which clock each comes from; dimensions for deployment type, endpoint and replica, model version, adapter version, tenant and API key; token counts (input, output and any cached input) and the tokenizer they were counted with; status and error classes; and rollups that keep honest percentiles after the raw records expire. Show how to answer: "time to first token percentiles per model version and deployment type per hour"; "output tokens per second during generation, per tenant and model version"; "queue time share of end-to-end latency on shared serverless models"; and "requests cancelled by the client after the first token, per model version".
sections.constraints: No prompt or output text in any record. Token counts are integers and match the model version's tokenizer. Durations are never negative and never measured across two machines' clocks without a stated correction. Rollups must allow percentiles to be combined across hours and tenants. A tenant sees only its own records and rollups.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, retention, streaming share, stage names and status classes are hypothetical; check current docs for any real product's metrics. Invoicing is out of scope; usage reporting reads the same token counts.
sections.criteria: A stated grain with tenant-visible requests and attempts linked; timestamps and durations defined per stage and per clock; dimensions for deployment, endpoint, replica, model version, adapter version, tenant and key; token counts tied to a tokenizer; cancellations and errors kept, not dropped; mergeable latency rollups that survive raw expiry; no content stored; volumes, partitioning and retention reasoned at the stated scale; tenant-scoped access; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a retry a new request?
clarifications.a: The platform may retry internally after a server failure; the tenant sees one request. Both views are needed.

clarifications.q: What is time to first token for a request that does not stream?
clarifications.a: Your choice; state it. In this exercise the server still records when the first token was produced.

clarifications.q: Do the router and the model server share a clock?
clarifications.a: No. They are separate machines; their clocks can differ by tens of milliseconds.

clarifications.q: What happens when the client disconnects mid-stream?
clarifications.a: The server stops generating and records a cancellation with the tokens produced so far.

clarifications.q: Are token counts comparable across models?
clarifications.a: Only within a tokenizer. Each model version names its tokenizer.

hints: Choose the grain first: one row per tenant-visible request, plus one per attempt for operations, linked by a request id.
Derive each duration from timestamps taken on one machine (or from monotonic durations measured there), and record which stage produced it.
Keep fixed-bucket latency histograms (or mergeable sketches) per hour and dimension, so percentiles survive the raw records' expiry and combine across groups.
followups: Walk one streamed request through routing, queueing, a server failure, an internal retry, the first token and a client disconnect. Which rows exist, and what durations does each carry?
The tenant's dashboard shows p99 time to first token for a week, and the raw records expired after {{raw_retention_days}} days. How is the p99 computed from what you kept, and how accurate is it?
A tenant asks why their output tokens on the latency dashboard differ from their usage report. Where can the two diverge in your model, and how do you make them agree?
At {{requests_per_day}} requests a day, estimate bytes per day at request grain and for the hourly rollups, and say how you partition and cluster each.

rules.ask: A few cold requests take 40 seconds. What does an hourly average hide, and how do you combine percentiles across hours from what you store?
The tenant sees one request; operations see two attempts. Which grain does the tenant's token count read, and how do you avoid counting tokens twice?
The router and the model server are different machines. How do you measure queue time without mixing their clocks?
These records never hold text. What do you keep instead to debug a slow request?
Two model versions use different tokenizers. Can you sum output tokens across them on one dashboard, and what do you label it?
