incidents: Queue time was computed as the model server's start time minus the router's receive time. After a clock drift on some servers, about 2% of requests showed negative queue time, and the hourly queue-time percentiles for shared serverless models dropped overnight with no change in load.

Client-cancelled streams were written with no completion time and were filtered out of the latency rollups. With {{streaming_share}} of requests streaming, the tenants whose users gave up fastest looked the healthiest on their dashboards.

Internal retries were written as separate tenant-visible requests. At about {{requests_per_day}} requests a day, a model server failure doubled one hour's output tokens on several tenants' dashboards, and the numbers no longer matched their usage reports.

templates.title: Calls after deprecation — per tenant, deprecated version and week, the calls made after the date in force, and the day the tenant first called the replacement
templates.subtopic: as-of lookup of versioned notices, midnight boundaries, ISO weeks, filtered first occurrence

sections.scenario: A cloud for open models deprecates model versions in its catalogue and names a replacement for each (this exercise's model; every model name, tenant and number is hypothetical). model_versions lists versions; deprecation_notices lists each notice sent for a version: notice_no (numbered in announcement order), announced_at, the deprecates_on date it gave and the replacement_id it named. {{notice_note}} requests holds every request from {{first_day}} to {{last_day}}: the tenant, the version called, the deployment (serverless or dedicated), a status (ok or error) and requested_at. The sample has {{tenants}} tenants, {{deprecated}} deprecated versions and {{request_rows}} request rows. The migration team wants to see, week by week, which tenants are still calling deprecated versions and whether they have started on the replacement.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns tenant_id, version_id, week_start, late_calls, replacement_calls, first_replacement_on: one row per tenant, deprecated version and week with at least one late call, ordered by tenant_id, version_id, week_start.

  • Only deployment = 'serverless' requests count anywhere in this report (in this exercise a catalogue deprecation applies to serverless calls; dedicated endpoints are out of scope).
  • The notice in force for a request is its version's notice with the highest notice_no whose announced_at is at or before requested_at. A request with no notice in force is never late.
  • A late call is a serverless request to a version, with any status, made at or after 00:00 UTC on the deprecates_on of the notice in force. A failed call still counts: it shows code that still points at the old version.
  • week_start is the Monday (UTC) of the late call's week, as a date.
  • replacement_calls is the tenant's serverless requests with status = 'ok' to the version's named replacement in that same week (0 when none).
  • first_replacement_on is the UTC date of the tenant's earliest serverless request with status = 'ok' to the named replacement, at any time in the data, before or after the deprecation date (NULL when there is none).
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Production has thousands of model versions, a notice history per version and billions of requests, partitioned by day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, versions, tenants, dates and counts; check current docs for any real deprecation policy. Every notice for a version names the same replacement. model_versions.family and released_on are context only. Tenants appear here only as ids; the report goes to the team that runs migrations, and each tenant would see only its own rows.
sections.criteria: Serverless filter applied to every part; the notice in force chosen per request by announced_at and notice_no; the midnight boundary inclusive; weeks starting Monday in UTC; late calls of any status; replacement calls and the first replacement day from successful serverless calls only, at any time; aggregation before joining so counts are not multiplied; deterministic ordering; can discuss partition pruning, pre-aggregation, corrected notices and replacement chains.

clarifications.q: A call arrives at exactly 00:00:00 UTC on the deprecation date. Is it late?
clarifications.a: Yes. The version is deprecated from that instant. A call one second earlier is not.

clarifications.q: A second notice postponed the date. Which date judges a call made before that notice was announced?
clarifications.a: The notice in force when the call was made. A call made after the first date had passed, but before an extension was announced, was late; calls after the extension are judged by its new date.

clarifications.q: The tenant called the replacement once on a dedicated endpoint before any serverless call. Does that set first_replacement_on?
clarifications.a: No. Only serverless calls count anywhere in this report.

clarifications.q: Does a failed call to the replacement count as the first call?
clarifications.a: No. Only a call with status = 'ok' shows the tenant running on the replacement.

clarifications.q: A tenant has late calls in one week and none in the next. Does the next week get a row?
clarifications.a: No. Only weeks with at least one late call.

hints: Find the notice in force per request with a LATERAL subquery (ORDER BY notice_no DESC LIMIT 1) over notices announced at or before the request.
Compare requested_at with deprecates_on::timestamptz, which is midnight UTC with the session in UTC, and bucket late calls with date_trunc('week', requested_at)::date.
Aggregate the late calls by tenant, version and week first, then join the replacement's successful serverless calls once, so the join cannot multiply the late-call counts.
followups: In production the requests table holds billions of rows partitioned by day. How would you restrict the scan, and what would you pre-aggregate so this report runs daily in seconds?
The migration team now wants tenants who called a deprecated version at least once in the last 7 days and have never succeeded on the replacement. Change the query.

A notice is later found to have been sent with the wrong date, and a corrected notice is issued. Should calls already judged late under the wrong notice stay late? Argue both ways, and say what the data model needs either way.
A replacement is itself deprecated a month later. Should a tenant that moved straight to the replacement's replacement count as migrated? Change the definition and the query.

rules.ask: A notice extended a date that had already passed. Is the version's latest notice the one in force for a call made before that notice was announced?
Your comparison works on dates. Is a call at 00:00:00 on the deprecation date late under your condition, and is one at 23:59:59 the day before?
Did you filter the late calls by status as well? What does a failed call to a deprecated version tell the migration team?
If you join every replacement call to every late call before counting, what happens to late_calls for a tenant with ten of each in one week?
Which day does your week start on, and what would another engine's default give for a Sunday call?

incidents: A deprecation was extended after its first date had passed. The report was re-run using each version's latest notice, and the calls made in the days before the extension, when tenants had been told the version was deprecated, vanished from the weekly figures the migration team had already shared.

The first version of this report counted dedicated-endpoint calls. Tenants running their own endpoints on the old version, out of scope for the catalogue deprecation, appeared at the top of the list of laggards.

templates.title: Per-tenant latency on shared serverless models — time to first token, throughput, noisy neighbours and honest percentiles at low volume
templates.subtopic: per-tenant latency, interference attribution, mergeable sketches, small samples

sections.scenario: A serverless inference service runs {{models}} open models that {{tenants}} tenants share. Each model is served by a pool of replicas, and each replica batches requests from many tenants together as they arrive (described generally). At peak the service handles about {{peak_rps}} requests per second. For every request the servers can record the tenant, the model version, input and output token counts, time spent queued, time to first token, generation time after the first token, the outcome and the replica that served it. Tenants want to see their own latency on each model; the platform team wants to know when one tenant's traffic is slowing everyone else on a model, and what to do about it. A percentile for a tenant is shown only when the window holds at least {{min_requests}} of that tenant's requests (this exercise's rule; check current docs).
sections.problem: Design per-tenant latency monitoring. Cover where each timing is measured and what exactly it includes; the event and its schema; aggregation per tenant, model version and minute, and how longer windows and the model-wide view are built from it; the tenant-facing console and API; how percentiles stay honest when a tenant has few requests; how a noisy neighbour is detected and attributed (which tenant, which model, what about its traffic); the actions the platform can take once one is found; alerts; retention; and how one tenant is kept from ever seeing another tenant's numbers.
sections.constraints: A tenant sees its own requests and, at most, the model-wide aggregate across all tenants; never another named tenant. Tenant views are fresh within one minute. Percentiles are never averaged across minutes, replicas or tenants. Below the {{min_requests}}-request floor the view shows counts and a stated reason, not a percentile. Prompts and outputs never enter the monitoring path; only counts and timings do.
sections.assumptions: Tenant counts, model counts, request rates and the floor are hypothetical. Servers have synchronised clocks; client-side timings are not available unless a tenant sends them. Batching and scheduling on a replica are described generally; you may assume the server can report, per replica and per second, which tenants' requests were in flight and how many input tokens each was processing.
sections.criteria: Server-side stages measured separately (queue, prefill to first token, generation) with honest labels about what each includes; one event per request with counts and timings only; exact counts plus mergeable sketches per tenant, model version and minute, with coarser views built by merging; a stated low-volume rule (floor, wider windows, counts and an interval instead of a point percentile); noisy-neighbour detection that attributes cause from per-replica records of what was in flight, not from correlation alone; proportionate actions (per-tenant limits, fair queuing, isolation, a dedicated endpoint offered) with communication; tenant scoping by construction in every query path; alerts on event time with lag awareness; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is time to first token measured on the server or the client?
clarifications.a: The server, from when the request was accepted to when the first token was sent. Say what that leaves out and how a tenant should read it.

clarifications.q: Does throughput mean tokens per second for the request or for the replica?
clarifications.a: For the tenant: output tokens per second for a request, measured after the first token. Replica throughput is a platform metric.

clarifications.q: Can the platform limit one tenant's traffic?
clarifications.a: Yes, by this exercise's per-tenant limits per model; you decide when a limit changes and who is told.

clarifications.q: Do tenants want per-request detail?
clarifications.a: They can look up their own requests by request id for a short retention period; the console shows aggregates.

clarifications.q: How many tenants are tiny?
clarifications.a: Most tenants send a few requests a minute to any one model; a few send thousands a second.

hints: Split time to first token into queue time and prefill time; interference from a neighbour shows up first in queue time, a tenant's own long prompts in prefill.
Keep one mergeable sketch per tenant, model version and minute, plus exact counts; every coarser view is a merge of sketches.
A noisy neighbour is a claim about cause. Record what each replica was doing per second so the claim can be checked, not only correlated.
followups: A tenant with 12 requests in the last hour asks for its p99 time to first token. What does the console show, and why?
Time to first token for most tenants on one model doubles for 20 minutes. Walk through how you find whether one tenant caused it, and what evidence you would show.
You decide to cap a tenant's concurrency on a model. How is that decided, applied and communicated, and how do you check it helped the others without hurting that tenant more than needed?
How do you merge per-replica, per-minute data into a tenant's hourly p95 and a model-wide p95 at {{peak_rps}} requests per second without shipping every request?
A tenant says your numbers are better than what their users experience. How do you help them reconcile the two?

rules.ask: Why can't you average per-minute p95 values to get a tenant's hourly p95, and what do you store instead?
A tenant sent 30 requests this hour. How many of them sit above its p99, and what does that number tell them?
What error does your sketch guarantee at p99, and is that error the same for a tenant with 40 requests as for one with 4 million?
The tenant you limited is paying for the traffic. What do you tell them, and what do you offer instead?
Two tenants' traffic rose at the same moment the latency did. How do you decide which one, if either, caused it?

incidents: One tenant starts sending long-context requests in bursts and accounts for 30% of one model's input tokens; time to first token p95 for every other tenant on that model rises from 0.4 s to 3 s for 20 minutes, mostly as queue time.

A tenant's console shows a p99 time to first token of 14 s computed from 9 requests, below the {{min_requests}}-request floor, because the API path that feeds the console skipped the floor; the tenant escalates to their account team.

During a traffic peak near {{peak_rps}} requests per second the aggregation pipeline falls 25 minutes behind; when it catches up, latency alerts fire for hundreds of tenants at once for a period that has already ended.

templates.title: Dedicated endpoint autoscaling and billing — replicas between a minimum and maximum, per-minute billing per running replica, and idle cost the customer can see
templates.subtopic: replica lifecycle events, minute-level metering, idle cost reporting

sections.scenario: Customers run {{endpoints}} dedicated endpoints, each serving one model on replicas that only that customer uses. Each endpoint has a minimum and a maximum replica count (the maximum here up to {{max_replicas}}). A new replica takes about {{load_minutes}} minutes to start and load the model before it can serve; a replica above the minimum is removed after {{idle_minutes}} minutes with no requests in flight. By this exercise's rule (check current docs), each replica is billed for every UTC minute from the minute it starts until the minute it stops, each started minute in full. Customers want endpoints that keep up with their traffic, a bill they can check minute by minute, and to know how much of what they pay for sat idle.
sections.problem: Design autoscaling and billing for dedicated endpoints. Cover the signals the autoscaler uses and the decision rule (scale up, scale down, stay); how load time is accounted for so the endpoint neither falls behind nor flaps; the replica lifecycle events (requested, starting, ready, draining, stopped) and who emits them; metering from those events into billed replica-minutes per endpoint and day; reconciliation of the meter with the replicas that actually exist; idle cost (replica-minutes with no requests in flight) shown to the customer with a recommendation; what happens when a scale-up cannot be satisfied quickly; and the console and API the customer uses.
sections.constraints: Every billed replica-minute traces to lifecycle events for a replica that existed; a replica is never billed twice for the same minute and never billed after its stop. Replica counts stay within the customer's minimum and maximum at all times. Billing totals are exact integers of replica-minutes; money is computed from them in integer minor units at a versioned price (all hypothetical). The customer's idle view and the invoice come from the same minutes.
sections.assumptions: Endpoint counts, load times, idle thresholds and prices are hypothetical, and the billing rule is this exercise's (check current docs). Replicas run on the platform's own infrastructure, described generally; whether a requested replica can start immediately depends on capacity you do not control.
sections.criteria: A scaling signal tied to demand (requests or tokens in flight, queue growth) rather than raw utilisation; a decision rule with hysteresis and cooldowns that accounts for load time, with its cost stated; lifecycle events as the single source of billing, emitted reliably (an outbox or equivalent) and reconciled against a listing of running replicas; minute bucketing done once, idempotent per replica and minute, with exact integer totals and versioned prices; idle minutes computed from the same minutes as the bill and turned into a recommendation; waiting-for-capacity shown and not billed; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, correction of bills and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is loading time billed?
clarifications.a: Under this exercise's rule, yes: billing starts at the minute the replica starts. Say how you show that to the customer.

clarifications.q: Can customers set the minimum to zero?
clarifications.a: Assume the minimum is at least one; a customer may stop the endpoint, which stops all replicas.

clarifications.q: What counts as idle?
clarifications.a: A replica-minute in which the replica had no request in flight at any moment. You may propose a better measure, but say how it is computed.

clarifications.q: Can the customer choose the scaling signal?
clarifications.a: They choose minimum, maximum and a target; the platform chooses how the signal is measured.

clarifications.q: What if a scale-up waits for capacity?
clarifications.a: The replica is requested but not started; it is not billed until it starts. The customer should see that it is waiting.

hints: The autoscaler and the meter should not share state: the autoscaler decides, the lifecycle events record what happened, and billing reads only the events.
Turn intervals into minutes once: a replica running from 10:03:40 to 10:07:05 touches the minutes 10:03 to 10:07, five billed minutes under this rule.
Scaling down after {{idle_minutes}} idle minutes while a replica takes {{load_minutes}} minutes to load is a control loop with a delay; think about hysteresis and cost before tuning numbers.
followups: Walk through one replica's life, from the autoscaler's decision to its last billed minute, and name every event and its timestamp.
Traffic arrives in bursts every 15 minutes. How does your rule behave, and what does it cost the customer compared with keeping one more replica running?
A stop event never arrives for one replica. How does the meter find out, and what does it bill?
What exactly does the idle view show, and how would a customer use it to change their minimum?
Scale-ups wait 40 minutes for capacity during a busy period. What does the customer see, what is billed, and how does the autoscaler avoid piling up requests it cannot satisfy?

rules.ask: GPU utilisation on an inference replica can be high while requests queue, or low while it is busy. Why is it a weak scaling signal here, and what do you use instead?
The queue grows now, but a new replica is ready only after {{load_minutes}} minutes. How far ahead does your rule have to look, and what does it do meanwhile?
The rule bills each started minute in full. Where in your pipeline do seconds become minutes, and how do you avoid billing a minute twice when two events fall in it?
Heartbeats from a replica stop for three minutes but it is still running. Do you stop billing, and how do you settle the minutes afterwards?
Your forecast scales up before a peak that does not come. Who pays for those replica-minutes, and how does the customer know why they ran?

incidents: Bursty traffic makes one endpoint add replicas that take {{load_minutes}} minutes to load and remove them after {{idle_minutes}} idle minutes; it cycles between 1 and {{max_replicas}} replicas 30 times in a day, and the customer's bill for that day triples while p95 latency barely improves.
During a control-plane restart, stop events for 140 replicas are lost, and the meter keeps billing them as running for up to 9 hours.
A customer whose endpoint sat at its minimum of 2 replicas with no requests in flight for most of a month disputes the invoice, saying nothing showed them it was idle.

templates.title: Many LoRA adapters on one dedicated endpoint — loading, eviction, cold loads measured, and per-adapter reports for the customer
templates.subtopic: placement and routing, cache eviction, cold-load measurement, per-adapter usage

sections.scenario: A customer runs one dedicated endpoint serving a base model on {{replicas}} replicas, with {{adapters}} LoRA adapters attached: their own fine-tunes, for example one per product line or per task. Each request names an adapter or none (the base model alone). Each replica can hold up to {{slots}} adapters in accelerator memory at once; an adapter that is not resident is loaded from host memory or object storage, which takes about {{cold_seconds}} seconds (hypothetical). Requests for different resident adapters can be batched together on a replica (described generally). The customer attaches and detaches adapters through the API as they retrain, and wants per-adapter traffic, latency and usage for their own internal chargeback.
sections.problem: Design adapter serving on the endpoint. Cover the adapter registry (immutable versions, the base model version each adapter was trained for, rank and target modules, checksums) and the compatibility check on attach; storage tiers and how adapters move between them; placement (which replicas hold which adapters) and request routing; the eviction policy and how hot adapters are replicated; how a cold load is defined, measured and attributed to the request that waited for it; detaching and replacing adapters while traffic flows; and the per-adapter report (requests, tokens, latency with cold and warm shown apart, load counts) through console and API.
sections.constraints: An adapter is never served on a base model version it was not trained for. Requests in flight when an adapter is detached complete; later requests get a documented error. Reports identify adapters by immutable version ids, with the customer's names shown beside them. Adapter weights are the customer's artefacts and are never inspected. Usage per adapter is for the customer's own reporting: the endpoint is billed by replica-minutes, not per adapter (this exercise's rule; check current docs).
sections.assumptions: Adapter counts, slot counts, load times and replica counts are hypothetical. All adapters on the endpoint target the same base model. Traffic across adapters is very uneven: a few adapters take most of it.
sections.criteria: An adapter registry with immutable versions, base-model compatibility checked on attach and again on load; tiered storage with explicit load events; adapter-aware routing with load balancing second and replication of hot adapters; an eviction policy that weighs frequency and recency, resists one-off bursts and respects pinning within a stated limit; cold loads defined, measured from events and shown apart from warm latency; safe detach and replace with versioned ids; per-adapter reports that sum to endpoint totals; adapters never inspected; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can one replica hold every adapter?
clarifications.a: Not in accelerator memory: only {{slots}} at a time. Host memory holds more; object storage holds all.

clarifications.q: Does a request for an adapter wait while it loads, or go elsewhere?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say what you do and what it costs.

clarifications.q: What is a cold load for reporting?
clarifications.a: A request that waited for its adapter to be loaded into accelerator memory. You decide how the wait is measured and whether queued requests behind it count too.

clarifications.q: Can the customer pin adapters so they are never evicted?
clarifications.a: You may offer it; say how pinning interacts with the slot limit.

clarifications.q: Are adapter names unique?
clarifications.a: Names are the customer's labels and can be reused after a detach; versions are not.

hints: Route by adapter first: send a request to a replica that already holds its adapter, and only then balance load.
The eviction policy is a cache policy with a cost per miss of about {{cold_seconds}} seconds; frequency and recency both matter, and a burst of one-off adapters should not evict the steady ones.
Record the load as its own event (adapter version, replica, start, end, reason) and join requests to it; a request's cold wait is then computed, not guessed.
followups: Walk through a request for an adapter that no replica holds. Where does it go, how long does it wait, and what does the report show?
One adapter suddenly takes 40% of traffic. How does placement respond, and how fast?
The customer detaches an adapter and attaches a retrained one under the same name within a minute. What happens to requests in flight, routing and the report?
How would you size {{slots}} slots across {{replicas}} replicas for {{adapters}} adapters, and what metric tells the customer they need more replicas?
The customer asks you to prove that adapter A's latency is worse because of cold loads and not because of the adapter itself. What do you show?

rules.ask: A nightly job touches every adapter once. What does least-recently-used do to the adapters your daytime traffic depends on?
An adapter was very busy last week and is now unused. How long does frequency keep it resident, and how do you age it out?
With {{adapters}} adapters and {{slots}} slots per replica, what share of requests would load their adapter cold under that routing?
Which adapters do you preload, how many slots does that take, and what happens to the rest when the customer pins too many?
A retrained adapter reuses the old one's name. Which id do routing and the report use, and how does the customer tell the two apart?

incidents: For a launch, the customer's traffic spreads evenly over all {{adapters}} adapters; with {{slots}} slots per replica, 45% of requests load their adapter cold, and p95 time to first token rises from 0.6 s to over {{cold_seconds}} seconds.

An adapter trained on an earlier version of the base model is attached after the endpoint was upgraded; every replica fails to load it, and its requests return errors for 30 minutes before anyone notices.

The customer detaches an adapter and attaches a retrained one under the same name; the per-adapter report for that day merges the two, and their own chargeback assigns the old adapter's traffic to the team that owns the new one.

templates.title: Customer artefacts for fine-tuning — datasets, checkpoints and adapters retained, expired and deleted in every copy, with a deletion receipt
templates.subtopic: artefact inventory and lineage, retention, verified deletion across copies, no access to contents

sections.scenario: {{tenants}} customers upload datasets for fine-tuning. On upload, the platform runs the validation the customer asked for (file format, required fields, turn order, lengths) and reports counts, line numbers and error codes. Jobs then train on the dataset and write checkpoints, and finish with a model or a LoRA adapter that the customer can deploy to an endpoint or download. Artefacts are stored with copies in {{regions}} regions for durability and are backed up; training nodes keep working copies (for example tokenised caches) while a job runs. By this exercise's rule (check current docs), checkpoints are kept {{retention_days}} days after a job ends unless the customer keeps them, a customer can delete any artefact at any time, every copy is gone within {{deletion_days}} days of the request, and the customer receives a deletion receipt.
sections.problem: Design the artefact lifecycle. Cover the inventory of artefacts and every copy of each (primary, regional copies, backups, caches on training nodes, models loaded on endpoints, exported downloads), and the lineage between them (dataset to job to checkpoints to model); retention and expiry; deletion on request across every copy, including backups and caches, and how it is verified; the deletion receipt (what was deleted, where, when, and what is kept and why); how a deployed model or adapter is handled when the customer deletes it; access control so that no person reads a customer's contents; how support helps a customer without seeing contents; and the audit trail.
sections.constraints: No person views a customer's dataset, checkpoint or adapter weights; the validator and the training job are the only processes that read contents, and validation output never contains content. A deletion receipt is issued only after every copy is verified gone or cryptographically unreadable. Billing records, receipts and counts may be kept after deletion; contents may not. Deleting a dataset does not delete models trained from it unless the customer asks; the customer is shown which ones exist.
sections.assumptions: Tenant counts, regions, retention periods and deletion targets are hypothetical. Storage is object storage with versioning and backups, described generally. Training nodes are shared between customers' jobs over time.
sections.criteria: An inventory where every copy and derived artefact is registered before use, with lineage from dataset to job to model; retention and expiry as policy with dates; deletion as a tracked workflow with a deadline, per-artefact or per-tenant keys destroyed for backups and stray copies, and verification before a receipt; explicit handling of deployed models and derived artefacts; no human access to contents by construction, validation output limited to counts, line numbers and codes, and access logs that prove it; support tooling built on metadata; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, containment, customer communication and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can backups be edited to remove one dataset?
clarifications.a: Assume backups are immutable snapshots that expire on a schedule; you need another way to make a deleted artefact unreadable within {{deletion_days}} days.

clarifications.q: What if the customer deletes a model that is deployed?
clarifications.a: Your choice: refuse until it is undeployed, or undeploy as part of the delete with explicit confirmation. Say which and why.

clarifications.q: Can support look at a failing dataset to help?
clarifications.a: No. Support sees validation results (counts, line numbers, error codes) and job metadata only.

clarifications.q: Do derived artefacts count?
clarifications.a: Yes: tokenised caches, shards and any file produced from the dataset are copies of it for deletion purposes.

clarifications.q: Does the receipt need to be signed?
clarifications.a: It should be verifiable by the customer later; you choose how.

hints: You cannot delete what you have not recorded: every write of an artefact or anything derived from it registers a copy in the inventory before it is used.
Encrypt each artefact (or each tenant's artefacts) with its own key; destroying the key makes every copy, including immutable backups, unreadable at once.
Treat deletion as a workflow with states (requested, keys destroyed, copies removed, verified, receipt issued) and a deadline, not a single call.
followups: Walk through deleting one dataset that three jobs trained on, one of which produced an adapter now deployed. What happens to each artefact, and what does the receipt say?
A training node crashes mid-job with a tokenised cache on its local disk. How does that copy get deleted, and how do you know it was?
How do you prove to an auditor that no person read a customer's dataset in the last year?
A customer's job fails validation and they ask support why. What can support see and say?
A customer asks for every copy of every artefact they ever uploaded to be deleted, today. How long does it take, what is kept, and why?

rules.ask: A soft-deleted dataset is still in storage. When does it become unreadable, and what does the receipt say in the meantime?
Backups are immutable for 35 days. How is a dataset deleted on day one unreadable in them by day {{deletion_days}}?
Who can use the per-tenant key, and what happens if the key service itself is restored from a backup?
An engineer needs to understand why many datasets fail one check. What can they see, and how do they get it without reading any customer's lines?
The nightly clean-up job fails for a week. Which deletion deadlines are missed, and who finds out?

incidents: An audit finds tokenised working copies of 300 deleted datasets left on training nodes' local disks for up to 40 days, beyond the {{deletion_days}}-day target, because jobs on those nodes crashed before their clean-up step.
A restore of one region's object storage after an operator error brings back 1,100 datasets that customers deleted during the previous month.
A change to the validator adds the first 200 characters of each failing line to error messages shown in the console and written to logs; it runs for two days before a customer points it out.

templates.title: The open-model catalogue lifecycle — new models added within days, versions, deprecations with notice, and per-tenant migration reporting
templates.subtopic: onboarding pipelines, acceptance checks, immutable versions and aliases, deprecation and migration

sections.scenario: The platform offers a catalogue of {{models}} open model versions, each available on serverless inference, on dedicated endpoints, or both. Model publishers release new open models often, and customers expect popular ones within days: the target here is {{onboard_days}} days from a public release to general availability (this exercise's target). A model entry has a family, a version, its licence as published, context length, the tokenizer and chat template, the serving variants offered, and prices. Older versions are deprecated with at least {{notice_days}} days' notice and a named replacement, then retired (this exercise's rule; check current docs). {{tenants}} tenants call catalogue models, some by an exact version id and some through a family alias.
sections.problem: Design the catalogue lifecycle. Cover intake of a new model (obtaining the publisher's public release, verifying checksums, recording the licence for the owners who review it, converting to serving variants); acceptance checks before release (tokenizer and chat template, deterministic smoke tests, performance targets, a check against public evaluation sets with synthetic expectations); the catalogue record as the one source for the API's model list, documentation, prices and billing; immutable version ids and how aliases move; deprecation (notice, named replacement, dates) and what happens to calls after retirement; per-tenant migration reporting, for the platform in aggregate and for each tenant about its own calls; and how a bad release is rolled back.
sections.constraints: A version id always means the same weights, tokenizer, template and serving variant; nothing about it changes after release except its lifecycle state. Every tenant that called a version in the last 30 days is notified of its deprecation through a contact they chose. No model is released before its licence has been recorded and reviewed by the people who own that decision; this design draws no legal conclusions. Prices and billing read the same catalogue record the API uses.
sections.assumptions: Model counts, tenant counts, onboarding targets and notice periods are hypothetical. Publishers release weights, tokenizers and templates publicly, and sometimes publish corrected revisions after release. Quality checks use public evaluation sets with expectations set by this exercise, not any real model's results.
sections.criteria: A staged onboarding pipeline with gates and measured durations against the {{onboard_days}}-day target; acceptance checks that cover tokenizer, template, determinism and performance, with honest limits on quality checks; one catalogue record feeding API, docs, prices and billing; immutable versions and aliases with a history and the resolved version on every request; deprecation with a notice floor, named replacement, verified delivery of notices and documented retirement behaviour; per-tenant migration reporting with aggregate views and tenant-scoped self-service; licence review recorded as a gate owned by the right people, with no legal conclusions in the design; rollback without breaking tenants who moved; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a publisher's corrected revision change our version?
clarifications.a: No; it becomes a new version. You decide whether and when an alias moves to it.

clarifications.q: What happens to a request for a retired version?
clarifications.a: Your choice of documented behaviour: an error naming the replacement, or a redirect. Say which, and why.

clarifications.q: Who decides a deprecation date?
clarifications.a: Product owners, using your migration data; the notice period is a floor.

clarifications.q: Who reviews licences?
clarifications.a: Legal and product owners. The pipeline records what was published and blocks release until review is recorded.

clarifications.q: Do tenants see each other in migration reports?
clarifications.a: No. The platform sees aggregates and per-tenant rows for outreach; a tenant sees only its own calls.

hints: Separate the pipeline into stages with explicit gates (intake, conversion, acceptance, review, pricing, release), so the {{onboard_days}}-day target is a measured path with known slow steps.
Treat aliases as pointers with a history: who moved them, when, from which version to which, so every request can be tied to the exact version that served it.
Migration reporting is a query over requests by tenant, version and week, plus the first call to the replacement; design the request record so it carries the resolved version id.
followups: Walk through a new open model from its public release to general availability. Which steps can run in parallel, and which gate usually takes longest?
A publisher fixes a tokenizer bug a week after release. What do you publish, and what happens to tenants on the alias and on the exact version?

With {{notice_days}} days to retirement, 15% of the deprecated version's traffic has not moved. What does your reporting show, and what do you do differently for the largest tenants and for the long tail?
On retirement day, what does a request to the retired version receive, and how do you measure the effect?
A new release turns out to be worse on one kind of task than its predecessor. How is that found, and how do you roll back without breaking tenants who already moved?

rules.ask: A tenant in production calls the family alias. You move it to a new version. What changed for them, and how did they find out?
The notice went to the address on the billing account, which nobody reads. How do you know a tenant actually received it?
A retired version's requests are sent to the replacement, whose output format differs slightly. Whose application breaks, and who learns about it first?
Your acceptance check passes but tenants report worse answers on their task. What did the check measure, and what would you add?
The API model list, the documentation and the pricing page disagree about one model's context length. Which is right, and how do you stop that recurring?

incidents: A newly added model is released with a chat template that drops the system turn; for two days tenants' outputs ignore their system instructions, and support receives 80 tickets before the cause is found.

On release day the family alias is moved to a new version; tenants calling the alias get a different output format, and 60 tickets arrive within a day from tenants who did not know they were on an alias.
{{notice_days}} days after notice, on retirement day, 400 tenants still send requests to the deprecated version; 150 of them never saw a notice because it went only to a billing contact.

templates.title: A licence change to a popular open model that customers already serve in production
templates.subtopic: decision rights, impact evidence, customer communication without legal conclusions

change: new terms that restrict some commercial uses above a stated size
new terms that add attribution and notice requirements for derived models
new terms that apply to future versions only, while earlier versions keep their old terms

sections.scenario: A popular open model family carries {{share}} of serverless traffic on the platform, and {{tenants}} tenants call it, fine-tune it or serve adapters on it. Its publisher announces {{change}}, taking effect in {{days}} days. Customers start asking support what this means for them, account teams want answers to give, and someone in a channel suggests switching every alias to a different model family tonight. You lead the team that owns the model catalogue and the usage data. Legal owns the interpretation of the terms; product owns what the platform offers.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover what you establish first and who you involve; the facts your team can supply (which tenants use which versions, through which paths: serverless, dedicated endpoints, fine-tunes, adapters) and how you supply them without exposing one tenant to another; what you say, and refuse to say, to customers and account teams before legal has concluded; the technical options you prepare (keeping earlier versions available if the owners decide so, a named alternative, help to migrate fine-tunes) and how you check each one; and how you avoid a rushed change that breaks customers. Then tell me about a real time an outside change you did not control forced a decision about something already in production, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You draw no legal conclusions and do not let anyone on your team draw them; the meaning of the terms is legal's to state. Customers' own obligations are theirs and their advisers'; the platform does not advise them. Every customer, figure and date is hypothetical.
sections.assumptions: The model, the terms and the timeline are hypothetical, as are the platform's possible responses.
sections.criteria: Separates interpretation (legal), platform response (product) and customer obligations (customers) and keeps to their own role; supplies precise usage facts quickly by tenant, version and path, scoped per audience; communicates early what is known (the announcement, the review, the next update date) without legal conclusions; resists a rushed production change and prepares checked options instead; plans for each plausible decision, including keeping earlier versions; follows through with notices and migration support once owners decide; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How long will legal take?
clarifications.a: They expect a first view within a week; they have asked for usage facts from you today.

clarifications.q: Can we tell customers what we think the terms mean?
clarifications.a: No. You can tell them what the publisher announced, link to it, say that the platform is reviewing it, and say when you will update them.

clarifications.q: Is switching aliases tonight possible?
clarifications.a: Technically, yes. Nobody has decided it, and some tenants call the alias in production.

clarifications.q: Do we know which tenants fine-tuned this family?
clarifications.a: Yes, from job metadata: base model and version per job, never the data.

hints: Separate three questions with three owners: what the terms mean (legal), what the platform offers (product), what each customer does (the customer).
Your team's contribution is precise facts fast: an inventory by tenant, version and path, scoped so each audience sees only what it needs.
A change made in a hurry to production aliases can do more harm than the thing it reacts to; prepare options, do not execute them.
followups: What does your first message to account teams say, and what does it deliberately not say?
Legal asks which tenants are affected. What exactly do you give them, and how do you keep it accurate as usage changes?
Someone senior wants the alias switched tonight "to be safe". How do you respond?
Legal concludes that earlier versions are unaffected. What changes in the catalogue, in notices and in your data?
In your real example, what decision was made, by whom, and what did you contribute to it?

rules.ask: You are not the owner of that interpretation. What happens if a customer acts on what you said and legal later concludes differently?
Some tenants call the alias in production with prompts tuned for this model. Who decided to change their outputs, and how did they learn about it?
What exactly does the message say before legal has concluded, and what does a customer do with it?
Account teams can see that report. How do you make sure each one sees only their own customers?
What did you personally decide or recommend, and to whom?

templates.title: Helping a customer whose fine-tune fails when you may not look at their data
templates.subtopic: diagnosis from metadata, reproducing with synthetic data, trust

failure: the training loss becomes NaN after a few hundred steps
the fine-tuned model mostly repeats its prompt back
the job passes validation and then fails with out-of-memory at a particular step
the fine-tuned model is no better than the base model on the customer's own checks

sections.scenario: A customer has run {{attempts}} fine-tuning jobs on the same base model and each time {{failure}}. They have a launch in {{deadline_days}} days and are frustrated; their message to support says "just look at our data and tell us what is wrong". By this exercise's rule (check current docs), no one at the platform reads a customer's dataset: the only processing of its contents is the validation the customer asked for and the training itself. You lead the team that owns the fine-tuning pipeline, and support has asked you to help.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover what you can learn without reading the data (job configs, validation results such as counts, lengths and error codes, training metrics, logs that carry no content); how you form and test hypotheses, for example by reproducing the failure with synthetic data of the same shape; what you can offer the customer so they can inspect their own data (tools, extra checks that report counts only, guidance); how you explain the rule to them without hiding behind it; what you do if the cause turns out to be the platform's; and how you handle the deadline. Then tell me about a real time you helped someone fix a problem in data or a system you were not allowed to see, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You never read the dataset, ask for it to be sent outside the documented process, or make an exception "just this once". Extra checks run only if the customer asks for them and report counts, line numbers and codes, not content. Every figure here is hypothetical.
sections.assumptions: The customer, base model and failure are hypothetical. The pipeline's validation results and training metrics are available to you for this job.
sections.criteria: Keeps the rule without hiding behind it and explains it to the customer and to support; diagnoses systematically from metadata with explicit hypotheses and predictions; reproduces with synthetic data of the same shape; equips the customer to inspect their own data precisely; checks whether the cause is the platform's and, if so, fixes it for everyone and says so; manages the deadline with honest options; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can the customer share a few examples with us?
clarifications.a: Only through the documented process, if one exists, and only by their explicit choice; assume for this scenario that there is none and you cannot create one this week.

clarifications.q: Have other customers seen the same failure?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet; you can look at aggregate job outcomes for the same base model and configuration.

clarifications.q: Is the support engineer on the customer's side or ours?
clarifications.a: Both; they want to help and are under pressure to make an exception.

clarifications.q: Can you change the pipeline for this customer?
clarifications.a: Only changes that would apply to every customer.

hints: Write down what each hypothesis predicts about the metadata you can see (length distributions, token counts, the step of failure, learning rate, method), then check.
A synthetic dataset with the same counts, lengths and structure reproduces many failures without any real content.
Give the customer a way to find the problem in their own data, with a precise description of what to look for.
followups: Which three hypotheses would you check first for {{failure}}, and what in the metadata would confirm or rule out each?
The support engineer suggests opening the dataset "only to look at the first ten lines". What do you say?
You reproduce the failure with synthetic data. What do you tell the customer, and what do you ask them to check?
The cause turns out to be a platform default that is wrong for long sequences. What changes for this customer and for everyone else?
In your real example, how did you work out the problem without seeing what you were not allowed to see?

rules.ask: The rule exists for every customer. What does it mean for the next customer, and for this one, if you make an exception today?
Which properties of their data does your synthetic set copy, and which can't it copy without reading their data?
Which of those did the customer choose, which did the platform default, and how did you tell?
What decision do you need from the person you escalate to?
What did you personally find or do?

templates.title: Deciding which of many newly released open models to support first
templates.subtopic: demand evidence, cost to serve, saying no, revisiting decisions

pressure: a large customer who says they will leave without one particular model
a competitor that announced support for three of them the same day
a researcher on your own team who is excited about a small model nobody has asked for

sections.scenario: In one month, {{releases}} new open models are released by different publishers. Your team can onboard about {{capacity}} of them properly in that month (conversion, acceptance checks, performance work, pricing and documentation), and each one added also costs serving capacity and on-call attention. Signals pull in different directions, including {{pressure}}. Product leadership owns the catalogue and asks you for a recommendation with evidence by the end of the week.
sections.problem: How do you decide? Cover the evidence you would gather (demand signals from tenants, expected traffic and cost to serve, effort to onboard, overlap with models already in the catalogue, licence status as recorded by the owners who review it, the publisher's track record of revisions), how you weigh it, how you present the recommendation and its uncertainty, how you treat {{pressure}}, what you tell the people whose model is not chosen, and how and when you revisit the decision. Then tell me about a real time you had to choose a few things to do from many reasonable ones, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot onboard more than about {{capacity}} properly this month; a rushed onboarding that skips acceptance checks is not an option. Licence questions are reviewed by legal and product owners; you only record their status. Every figure is hypothetical.
sections.assumptions: The models, publishers, customers and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Gathers comparable evidence with stated uncertainty and the least reliable signal named; counts long-term cost to serve and maintain, not only onboarding; presents a clear recommendation with ranges and the decision owner's role respected; treats pressure on its evidence; communicates no-for-now decisions with reasons and a revisit date; sets triggers to revisit and learns from misses; real example with what was declined and how it landed, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do we have demand data?
clarifications.a: Some: requests for unknown model names in the API, support tickets, waitlist sign-ups and account team notes. All are noisy.

clarifications.q: Can we add a model in a limited preview?
clarifications.a: Yes, with clear labelling, if product agrees; it still takes onboarding effort.

clarifications.q: How costly is a model nobody uses?
clarifications.a: It takes serving capacity, testing on every platform change and a later deprecation.

clarifications.q: Is the large customer's claim verified?
clarifications.a: It came through their account team; you do not know their volume on that model.

hints: Turn noisy signals into a comparable estimate per model, with ranges, and say which signal you trust least.
Count the long-term cost of adding a model, not only the onboarding effort.
Decide in advance what new evidence would change the choice, and when you will look.
followups: What would your one-page recommendation look like, and what goes in its first three lines?
How do you treat {{pressure}} in the decision, without either ignoring it or letting it decide alone?
Two models are close on every measure. How do you break the tie?
A month later, one model you skipped has become very popular. What do you do, and what do you learn?
In your real example, what did you decide not to do, and how did the people who wanted it react?

rules.ask: Who chose the weights, and would the ranking change if a reasonable colleague chose different ones?
How do you know how much traffic that customer would actually send, and what would you need to see before trusting it?
What evidence do you have that tenants choose a platform for that, rather than for something else?
Your team can do {{capacity}} properly. What gets worse if you try to do more?
What did you personally recommend, and what did the decider change?

templates.title: Telling customers they are paying for idle capacity, when that lowers revenue
templates.subtopic: customer-facing transparency, stakeholder alignment, revenue trade-offs

objection: a sales leader worried about the quarter
a finance partner who says customers chose their own settings
a product manager who wants to ship it only as an opt-in report

sections.scenario: Your team built the data behind dedicated endpoint billing. Analysis shows that across customers about {{idle_share}} of billed replica-minutes had no requests in flight: endpoints kept at a minimum higher than their traffic needed, replicas left running after tests, and scale-down settings that rarely trigger. You propose an idle view in the console with recommendations, and a monthly notice for endpoints idle most of the time. Finance estimates that if customers act on it, revenue from dedicated endpoints falls by about {{revenue}} over the next year. The strongest objection comes from {{objection}}.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you make sure the analysis is right before arguing from it; how you frame the decision for the people who own it, including the long-term case (trust, retention, customers who would otherwise leave quietly) alongside the short-term revenue; how you address {{objection}} on its merits; what you would accept as a compromise and what you would not; how the feature is built so its numbers match the invoice; and how you would measure the result. Then tell me about a real time you argued for something right for customers that cost your organisation something, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not own pricing or the decision to ship; product and the business owners do. Everything you show customers must match the invoice minute for minute. Every figure is hypothetical.
sections.assumptions: The analysis, revenue estimate and stakeholders are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Verifies the analysis, including deliberate idle capacity, before arguing from it; frames a long-term versus short-term decision honestly with uncertainty, for the people who own it; engages the objection on its merits; distinguishes acceptable compromises (how it ships) from unacceptable ones (customers kept from facts about their own bill); builds numbers that tie to the invoice; defines how success is measured; respects the decision while making disagreement visible through the right channel; real example with cost, decider and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are customers being billed wrongly?
clarifications.a: No. They are billed correctly under the rules for what they ran.

clarifications.q: Have customers complained?
clarifications.a: A few have, after finding idle endpoints themselves; some of them moved workloads elsewhere.

clarifications.q: Could the analysis overstate idle time?
clarifications.a: Possibly: an endpoint kept warm for latency may be idle by your measure and still worth it to the customer.

clarifications.q: Who decides?
clarifications.a: The product owner, with the business owner for dedicated endpoints.

hints: Check the idle measure against cases where idle capacity is deliberate, and say how the view treats them.
Put long-term and short-term effects in the same units where you can, and state what you cannot quantify.
A good compromise changes how it ships, not whether customers can find the truth about their own bill.
followups: How do you check that {{idle_share}} is right, and what would make you lower it?
How do you answer {{objection}} without dismissing it?
The decision is to ship only an opt-in report. Do you accept it, and what do you do next?
How would you know a year later whether the feature helped or hurt the business?
In your real example, what did it cost, who decided, and what happened afterwards?

rules.ask: Put a number on what happens to retention if customers find the idle cost themselves. How sure are you of it?
Who finds an opt-in report, and are they the customers who most need it?
How does your view tell a deliberately warm endpoint from a forgotten one, and what does it recommend for each?
What do you bring, to whom, and how do you keep working with the people who disagreed?
What did you personally say, and to whom?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a cloud that fine-tunes and serves open models
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, metering per tenant, artefact lifecycle and model versions

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: usage metered per tenant and model version that matches the invoice exactly
each customer's datasets and checkpoints deleted in every copy, with a receipt
per-tenant latency that stays honest for tenants with few requests
every request traceable to the exact model version and adapter that served it
scale: hundreds of open models and thousands of model versions
billions of inference requests a day

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for a cloud that fine-tunes and serves open models, at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The open-model cloud setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example idempotent usage keyed by request id with versioned prices and one rounding step tied to the invoice; an inventory of every copy with per-artefact keys and verified receipts; mergeable sketches with a low-volume floor; immutable model and adapter version ids resolved on every request); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be an ML or inference system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the re-examination, start from one inference request or one uploaded dataset: which ids and timestamps it carries, where copies of it end up, and which of them the new requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
A request says only the model's family name. How does your record show the exact version that served it a month later?
Where do copies of one customer's data end up in your system, including caches and backups, and how would you prove they are all gone?
One tenant sent 14 requests yesterday. What latency figure does your system show them, and is it honest?
